# Contained in this
# little volume.

1. Two books by Levinus Lemnius on the **hidden miracles of nature**. <note>Levinus Lemnius (1505–1568) was a Dutch physician. This work, *De occultis naturae miraculis*, was a popular Renaissance text exploring natural wonders, medicine, and the "secret" workings of the physical world.</note>
2. Dialogues on the **chemical art**. <note><term>Chemical Art</term>: A historical term for alchemy. These dialogues likely discuss the transmutation of metals and the spiritual refinement of the alchemist.</note>
3. Niphus on **auguries**. <note>Agostino Nifo (c. 1473–1538) was an Italian philosopher. His work on "auguries" deals with the interpretation of omens and the art of divination.</note>
4. The new **Hieroglyphics** of Horus Apollo. <note>Horus Apollo (also known as Horapollo) was the supposed author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs. During the Renaissance, these were viewed not just as writing, but as sacred, mystical symbols of divine truths.</note>

# THE PRIVILEGE
## decree. <note>original: "sententia"; in this legal context, it refers to the formal decision or summary of the grant.</note>

It is provided by the authority of Philip, King of the Spains, <note>Philip II of Spain, who at this time also ruled the Netherlands as the Duke of Burgundy.</note> that no one else except William Simon may print this book, *The Hidden Miracles of Nature*, before the end of four years, or sell it if printed elsewhere. Whoever shall do otherwise will be fined the penalty assessed in the Decree, as is more fully evident in the Decree itself, given at Brussels, on the second day before the Nones of April. <note>Using the Roman calendar, the "second day before the Nones of April" is April 4th.</note>

->1559.<-

->Signed by Ph. de Lens.<- <note>Philippe de Lens was a secretary to the King in the administrative councils of the Spanish Netherlands.</note>

<summary>This page presents the legal copyright (privilege) granted by King Philip II of Spain to the publisher William Simon, protecting the book from unauthorized reprinting for four years.</summary>

# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN,
## of the highest virtue and dignity, Master Matthias van Mont
### of Heeswijk, especially revered Prelate at Middelburg, <note>original: "Metelliburgum"; the Latin name for Middelburg in the province of Zeeland, Netherlands.</note>
### Levinus Lemnius, Physician, sends heartiest greetings.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'L' featuring intricate scrolling vine motifs and foliage within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

*Lysander the Spartan,* <note>A famous Spartan admiral and politician (d. 395 BCE).</note> *having once observed and marveled at the skill of Cyrus, King of the Persians, and his diligence in the layout of rural affairs—specifically, fields neatly planted with trees and arranged in rows of a quincunx* <note>A geometric pattern of five points, like the dots on a die; a popular arrangement for orchards in antiquity.</note> *—said: “Truly and rightly, Cyrus, they call you blessed, because that fortune of yours is joined to your virtue.” But I, magnificent Sir, ought to admire and look up to you for a more just cause: because you have resolved to devote such great effort and such great expense to constructing and furnishing a Library, than which there will be none more richly stocked among the Netherlanders.* <note>original: "Belgas"; referring generally to the people of the Low Countries.</note> *By this deed, it can scarcely be said what an increase has come to your virtue, or how much dignity and solid praise you will win for yourself among all people. A few years ago, in the sacred temple over which you preside, a skillfully wrought Mausoleum was erected, a gift and monument dedicated to the soul of King William.* <note>This refers to William II, Count of Holland and King of the Romans (d. 1256), whose remains were re-interred in a grand tomb in the Abbey of Middelburg in 1548.</note> *From which the Batavians* <note>The "Batavi" were an ancient Germanic tribe; the term was used in the Renaissance as a scholarly name for the Dutch.</note>

<summary>In this dedication, the physician Levinus Lemnius praises Matthias van Mont for establishing a magnificent library in Middelburg and mentions the recently constructed tomb of King William II of Holland.</summary>

# EPISTLE
<meta>catchword: ius</meta>

...of the August Prince and Emperor-designate, the second of that name, <note>Likely referring to Emperor Charles V or Maximilian II; "August" was a standard title for the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> a long lineage and series of descendants was brought forth; and the splendor of nobility was attained by your especially dear Lord Philibert of Serooskerke and Stavenisse, <note>Philibert van Serooskerke (d. 1579) was a prominent Zeeland nobleman and contemporary of Lemnius.</note> a man illustrious not only for the fame of his family, but for his skill in languages and knowledge of affairs. Shrines were constructed there, and sumptuous seats elaborately and elegantly carved. Paintings were displayed to delight and feed the eyes, depicted graphically and entirely to the life; these (to speak frankly) are both an ornament to such a famous and majestic place, and they continually renew the memory of those who saw to their completion, and to whose name and grandeur they are consecrated. Not to mention so many tapestries and purple-dyed hangings,

<margin>From Virgil's *Aeneid*.</margin>
— So many garments stiff with gold and gems... <note>original: "Tot Pallas auro gemmisq; rigentes"; a reference to the rich fabrics of antiquity described by Virgil.</note>

Meliboean purple ran in a double Meander pattern. <note>original: "Purpura meandro duplici melibœa cucurrit"; Meliboean refers to a Thessalian town famous for purple dye, and a "Meander" is a winding decorative border.</note>

But your most holy endeavor will deserve more praise, and a grateful posterity will proclaim your virtues somewhat more abundantly, because you are gathering such a great heap of books, because,

### DEDICATORY EPISTLE

*...tly, that in the furthest reaches of the Ocean you have seen to it that such a distinguished library be adorned and furnished: truly a magnificent work, and clearly a royal one, than which no virtue, no dignity, and no reputation can be made either more increased, or more remarkable, or finally more stable. For the memory of such a great thing will not fade with any age, nor will it be destroyed by any injury of time. A proof of this is Ptolemy Philadelphus,* <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus (308–246 BCE), the Pharaoh of Egypt who greatly expanded the Great Library of Alexandria.</note> *who gained a memorable name through that most well-furnished library of Alexandria, and clearly protected himself from the injury of oblivion. Therefore, so that such great glory and grandeur might become known to all, and the honor of your name might be spread among all the most learned, I thought that these* <term>ἀναιτιολογητα</term> <note>original Greek: *anaitiologēta*; meaning "things without an assignable cause." Lemnius uses this to describe natural phenomena that seem miraculous because their causes are hidden.</note>, *or hidden miracles of nature, should be dedicated to you. For indeed, my mind only then began to grow warm and be stirred to complete these things, when I understood that such a noble undertaking was being begun by you. And since I saw so many things thus illustrated and refined by men of our profession, that the Medical art seems to have attained all its luster and glory, lest some sharper critic sing that line of the Comic poet:* <note>A reference to the Roman playwright Terence, from the prologue of his play *Eunuchus*.</note> *Nothing is said that has not been said before:* <note>original Latin: "Nihil dictum, quod non dictũ prius."</note>

### EPISTOLA

...nor have I devised a common or trivial subject, but rather one in which I have strived to work with such diligence that the reading will be not only useful, but also pleasant. For indeed, as Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BCE – 24 CE) was a Greek geographer and philosopher who argued that literature should provide pleasure to entice the reader into learning.</note> testifies, such pleasure is the "bait" of reading and learning; it ensures that less boredom arises and that you may persist in your reading more intently. Therefore, so that these things might not be a source of distaste to scholars, I have endeavored to entice and hold the reader’s attention both through the novelty of the subject matter and, as much as possible, through the purity of my language.

Many things were brilliantly conceived and divinely described by great minds in previous centuries; however, many of those works began to be neglected and held in contempt because they were devoid of any rhetorical ornament or refinement of language. Truly, those authors took too little care for their own legacy or for the convenience of students. For, as Cicero says, <margin>Tusculan Disputations, Book 1</margin> to commit one's thoughts to writing when one can neither arrange nor illustrate them, nor entice the reader with any delight, is the mark of a man who intemperately abuses both his leisure and literature. As Fabius <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, known as Quintilian, a celebrated Roman teacher of rhetoric.</note> so skillfully writes: <margin>Book 2, chapter 17</margin> "Even though the precepts for living are honorable in themselves, they nevertheless carry more weight in shaping minds whenever the clarity of speech illuminates the beauty of the subject." <note>original: "Ipsa vitæ præcepta licet per se honesta sint, plus tamen momenti obtinere ad formādas mentes, quoties pulchritudinem rerum claritas orationis illuminat."</note>

<summary>In this section of the preface, the author justifies his focus on literary style, arguing that scientific or philosophical truths are more effective when presented with "ornament" and clarity. He cites classical authorities like Strabo, Cicero, and Quintilian to emphasize that a pleasing prose style prevents reader boredom and ensures the preservation of knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>rhetoric, elocution, Strabo, Cicero, Quintilian, literary style, education, aesthetics, classical authority</keywords>

This page expands on that theme, citing Horace and Galen to justify the author's attention to clear and elegant language even when discussing technical or medical subjects.</meta>

### DEDICATORY [LETTER]

<margin>iiij</margin>

Nor did *Horace* <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BCE) was a leading Roman lyric poet. He is often cited for his views on the dual purpose of literature: to teach and to please.</note> sing only for himself and for men of his own kind:

<margin>In *The Art of Poetry*.</margin>
> *Poets aim either to benefit, or to delight,* <note>original: "Aut prodesse volunt, aut delectare Poëtæ"</note>
> *Or to say things both pleasing and suitable for life at once.* <note>original: "Aut simul & iucunda, & idonea dicere vitæ"</note>

Indeed, this applies also to *Physicians*, as well as those who bring cultivation to the soul and shape the mind for piety. For men embrace more eagerly, and there flows more effectively into their minds, those things which are structured by their own inner power and illuminated by the brilliance of speech. And although 
<margin>On the Properties of Foodstuffs.</margin>
*Galen* <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his works formed the basis of medical knowledge for over a millennium.</note> thinks that one should not cling too anxiously to words, and disapproves of an empty heap of words beneath which there is no substance or meaning: it is nevertheless better to join eloquence with wisdom <term>prudentia</term> <note>The author uses the Latin "prudentia," which in this context means "practical wisdom" or "sound judgment."</note>. Let it certainly be—and I agree without controversy—that the knowledge of things is more powerful than the knowledge of words, 
<margin>*On the Orator*, Book 2.</margin>
and even to *Cicero* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was Rome’s greatest orator. He argued that an orator must be a master of the subject matter, not just a stylist.</note> himself, unadorned wisdom was more desirable than foolish loquacity; yet a matter must be explained with appropriate and clear words. And although the subject matter which I have undertaken to treat rejects the elegance of oration, I nevertheless hope that I shall achieve this: that I may not seem to have treated it entirely coldly or feebly. Furthermore, as far as the explanation of things is concerned, I do not want it to be a disadvantage to me, or [be attributed] by anyone to audacity...

<meta>catchword: teme- [likely: temerity/rashness]</meta>

<summary>The author justifies his focus on clear and elegant writing by citing classical authorities like Horace, Galen, and Cicero, arguing that medical and moral truths are more effective when presented with eloquence. He acknowledges that while the facts are most important, style prevents the work from being "cold" or "feeble."</summary>

### THE LETTER

<meta>catchword: rendi</meta>

...and to be accused of rashness, because I undertake to explain abstruse things for which no certain method can be found: since, while shrinking from investigating and scrutinizing the majesty of the **Supreme Deity** <note>original: "supremi Numinis maiestate"</note>, I instead dig out the causes of nature and physical things. It is through these causes that the Majesty of the **Creator** shines forth in us, and our wonder increases. 

I thought these works should be dedicated especially to your name, most distinguished **Prelate** <term>Antistes</term> <note>A title for a high-ranking religious official, such as a bishop or abbot.</note>, because several illustrious men of consular rank testified in a crowded circle of bystanders that you have a singular inclination of mind toward **Lemnius** <note>The author, Levinus Lemnius (1505–1568), refers to himself here in the third person. He was a prominent Dutch physician and author of works on natural philosophy.</note>, and that you are greatly delighted by the reading of his little books—so much so that once the Assembly <note>Likely a reference to a specific political or ecclesiastical meeting, such as a Diet or Council.</note> was concluded, you took care to have me summoned once and then again, so that we might enjoy each other’s company. 

Moved by these things, and led by the excellence of your virtue which has raised you to this peak of honor, I wished to earn your favor with these nighttime studies <note>The author uses the term "lucubrationibus," implying scholarly work conducted by lamplight.</note> of ours, to please you, and to offer evidence of my ready and willing devotion toward you. I hope and auspiciously predict that, after **Jean Fernel** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a legendary French physician who served King Henry II and is credited with introducing the term "physiology" into the medical lexicon.</note>, Physician to the Most Christian **King of the Gauls** <note>The King of France.</note>, whose elegance of speech and method of discourse <note>original: "disse-rendi"</note> uniquely moves me...

<summary>In this dedication, Levinus Lemnius defends his study of natural philosophy as a way to honor God and acknowledges the patronage of a high-ranking official who admires his work. He expresses his admiration for the style of the famous French physician Jean Fernel.</summary>
<keywords>Levinus Lemnius, Jean Fernel, natural philosophy, theology, patronage, eloquence, medical history, King of France</keywords>

->DEDICATORY<-
<sig>v 2</sig>
<meta>The catchword "rendi" from the previous page completes the word "conquirendi" (seeking out) or "explicandi" (explaining) the subtlety of nature.</meta>

...subtlety of [explaining] <note>original: "rendi subtilitas"</note>: after *Girolamo Cardano* and *Fracastoro*, men of profound erudition, I feel I have not undergone this labor in vain. This is true even though I began to work on these matters before their writings were published or presented to me for examination. 

A most reliable witness of this, among others, can be *Master Andreas Vesalius*, *Imperial Physician* <note>Vesalius (1514–1564) was the most famous anatomist of the Renaissance and physician to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>, than whom no one within human memory is more practiced in the field of Anatomy; he earnestly encouraged me to complete these works. He did so together with the illustrious man *Master Nicolaus Bonardus*, his brother-in-law <note>original: "sororio"</note>, who by the munificence and liberality of the *Emperor* <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> obtained the Prefecture <term>Præturam</term> <note>The office of a high-ranking magistrate or administrative official.</note> of the city of *Zierikzee*. 

But there is no reason for me to be greatly troubled [by critics], since I am following in no one else's footsteps but am entering upon a different way of treating this subject. 

Meanwhile, most esteemed **Prelate** <term>Antistes</term> <note>A title for a high-ranking cleric, such as a bishop or provost.</note>, take care of your health, and do not exhaust yourself more than is sufficient with either public or private business. Remember that something must be granted to the body, by whose protection and support the soul itself is sustained. 

<margin>A Comparison.</margin> For if we take care that our houses are not marshy and damp, nor crack with fissures, nor become passable to winds and rains...

->E P I S T L E<-

[so that] they may be <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's thought on caring for the physical members of the body.</note>, so that health might be more unimpaired, and less exposed to diseases: how much more is it right to provide for the body, whose dwelling-place and service the soul itself uses? For this reason, I consider it praiseworthy for those who perform public duties, and those who are devoted to letters <note>This refers to scholars, authors, and students of the humanities.</note>, to occasionally set aside their work, and occupy themselves from time to time with grafting trees and arranging gardens. For business and the study of literature, while they bring cultivation to the mind, they also bring harm to the body; and as *Fabius* <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 AD), a Roman rhetorician who discussed the mental strain of study.</note> says, "thought affects the senses more than physical exhaustion." Since even the great King Solomon experienced this, with no small cost to his health:

<margin>Ecclesiastes 12</margin>
> "Of making many books," he said, "there is no end; and much study <note>original: "frequensque meditatio"</note> is a weariness of the flesh."

For this reason, he took care to build gardens and orchards <note>original: "viridaria"</note> so that he might dispel the burdens of business and the weariness of study. Therefore, all who desire to consult the best interests of their health should not be reluctant to take up such exercises <term>exercitamenta</term> <note>Meaning physical activities or pastimes used for health and recreation.</note>, since the nobility of old and the ancient heroes were especially occupied with them whenever they were permitted to take a breath from public duties and allow themselves some relaxation. Thus, besides the leaders of the Hebrew nation, Mi-

<meta>This page continues the list of historical figures who found health and restoration in gardening and rural life, specifically connecting these ancient examples to the dedicatee's own estate and contemporaries.</meta>

->DEDICATORY<-

<meta>catchword: are [original: sunt]</meta>

[Mith]ridates <note>The text begins with the completion of the name Mithridates VI of Pontus (135–63 BC), who was famous for his study of botany and poisons.</note>, King of Pontus, Lysimachus, Eupator, Gentius, King of the Illyrians, and Artemisia, wife of Mausolus, King of Caria <note>Artemisia II of Caria (died c. 350 BC), known for her grief and her botanical knowledge; she is the namesake of the herb genus *Artemisia*.</note>, were all delighted by the study of cultivating herbs and trees. In the same way, Marcus Curius <note>Manius Curius Dentatus, a Roman hero known for his frugality and love of farming.</note>, after the defeat of Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes, used to enjoy himself by living a rustic life in a certain country villa. So too did Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus and Marcus Valerius Corvinus; drawn by the pleasantness of plants, they grew old in the countryside, far from the noise and ambition of city life.

In this same manner, your estate at Westhonia <note>Refers to the country estate of the dedicatee, Matthias van Mont.</note> refreshes you from time to time; it provides a space for breathing in the retreat of a most healthy location once you have finished with heavy and serious affairs. It can hardly be expressed what agility of body, what vigor of spirit, what mental alacrity, what inexhaustible youthfulness, and finally what a firm old age—by no means exhausted or burdensome to the body—is enjoyed by those who have completely dedicated themselves to these kinds of delights.

For this reason, Lord Antonius à Burgo and Oudeweruio <note>Likely referring to a contemporary nobleman or official, possibly of the de Bourgogne or similar noble lineage in the Low Countries.</note>—a man of exceptional sincerity in addition to his noble character—seems to me to be acting excellently and according to the custom of our ancestors. The same is true for many others who adorn their nobility with the study of letters: by constructing estates and villas situated in healthy locations, they devote themselves Earnestly to these diversions...

are dedicated, and healthily exercise their minds with studies and their bodies with hunting. But now it is time, O most upright man, that I attempt to unearth the miracles of nature. # TO THE CANDID READER
## PREFACE BY L. LEMNIUS, PHYSICIAN.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' featuring scrolled foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

**D**uo are the instruments of the arts which serve the utility and use of mankind, by which all things are customarily strengthened and established: *Reason and Experience. For by these, Medicine itself—and most other arts besides the Mathematical ones—are supported. Indeed, those things which are to gain credit with men of exact and refined judgment ought to be measured by this rule <note>original: "amussim"; a carpenter’s rule or level, signifying precision.</note> and tested against this touchstone <note>original: "lapidem Lydium"; a Lydian stone used to test the purity of gold or silver.</note>. For what greatness could a physician show if he should strive to prove by reason alone that herbs and medicines obtain effective results, unless he confirms it by experience? Conversely, with what confidence could he rely on experience—which the unthinking rashness of the Empirics <note>A group of medical practitioners who relied solely on practical experience and trial-and-error, often criticized by university-trained physicians for lacking theoretical foundation.</note> declares to be deceitful and dangerous when applied without judgment—unless reason supports it? And although it might be considered sophistical to demand a reason against the testimony and evidence of experience, yet no one of sound judgment, and who weighs the choice of things carefully, would ever grant assent to an experiment, or endure to try it rashly, unless it be confirmed and supported in every way by reason. Yet I cannot deny or turn away from the fact that there are many things in nature so hidden and abstruse, and with such a latent and blind effect, that it would be rash to attempt to approach them by reason,*
<margin>Book 6, chapter 34.</margin>
*or to explain the cause of the deed. These very things are called "unexplainable" <note>original Greek: ἀναιτιολόγητα (anaitiologēta)</note> by Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist whose work was the primary source for herbal medicine for 1,500 years.</note>, that is, destitute of reason.*

<summary>In this preface, the physician Levinus Lemnius introduces the two pillars of medical knowledge: Reason and Experience. He argues that while experience provides the evidence, reason is necessary to validate and safely apply medical treatments, though he admits some natural phenomena remain beyond human explanation.</summary>
<keywords>Levinus Lemnius, medical methodology, Reason vs Experience, Empiricism, Dioscorides, philosophy of science, 16th-century medicine</keywords>

--- Page 34 ---
<meta>This page continues the Preface from Levinus Lemnius. The previous page ended mid-sentence with "wou...", which connects here to the Latin "tuta" (likely from "instituta," meaning established or settled). The author is transitioning from the necessity of combining reason and experience to the problem of phenomena that seem to defy both.</meta>

# TO THE READER

<margin>Hidden properties.</margin>
...ld trust things that are not **safely established**, and are devoid of the knowledge of causes, which exhibit no manifest demonstration to the sense or the intelligence; and for that reason, they are called **Occult properties** <note>original: "Occultæ proprietates"; a term in Renaissance science for powers of nature—like magnetism or the healing properties of herbs—that could be observed but not explained by the four elements.</note> by Physicians. Indeed, they believe that something intervenes in things of this kind, whether from the course of the stars and the path of the radiating planets, or from divine will, or from the concretion and mixture of the elements, or finally from the power and **specific form** <note>The "form" of a thing was its essential nature that gave it its unique characteristics.</note> of the whole substance. Since we cannot grasp these things by reason or the judgment of the mind, we relegate them to hidden essences and secret properties; by such a refuge we escape, and extricate ourselves from that **Labyrinth**.

But as for me, in order to stimulate the minds of learned men toward the demonstrations and the unearthing of the causes of such things, I shall strive with all my might to elicit a reason by probable and artful conjecture, or to touch the mark by aiming as closely as possible. I confess, there are many things in the works of nature whose origins are undiscovered and wrapped in thick obscurities; however, a probable reason for these can be devised, and the cause of the effect can be rendered—if not clearly and transparently, certainly with likelihood.

For example: the **Basilisk** <note>A legendary reptile reputed to be king of serpents and said to have the power to cause death with a single glance.</note> kills a man by sight. Who, trained in the works of nature, would not know that this happens from the emanating noxious vapors <note>original: "expirationibus"; literally "breathings." Science of this era often explained "magic" as the physical movement of invisible particles or spirits.</note> which it exhales slowly and secretly for the destruction of man? For not only the **Regulus** <note>original: "Regulus"; another name for the Basilisk, meaning "little king."</note>, but almost every kind of wild beast is hostile to man and delights in inflicting death with its breath and hiss. Thus the sight of a **wolf**, provided it stands near to a man, induces hoarseness by the opening of its mouth and its poisonous breath, and so...

<margin>⁜
* + .</margin>

<summary>Levinus Lemnius discusses "occult properties"—natural phenomena without obvious causes—and argues that physicians should use "probable conjecture" to find rational explanations for them, using the basilisk's deadly gaze as an example of toxic exhalations.</summary>
<keywords>occult properties, natural philosophy, basilisk, medical theory, causality, toxicology, lupine hoarseness, Levinus Lemnius</keywords>

--- Page 35 ---
<meta>This page continues the Preface by the Dutch physician Levinus Lemnius. On the previous page, the author discussed the difficulty of explaining "occult properties" in nature. This page picks up mid-argument, likely discussing the physical effects of various "emanations" or breaths, transitioning into a discussion on how contagion is physically transmitted through the air and the eyes.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

...yet it does not take away the voice. Likewise, during the time of their flow, the **menstruating** female sex <note>Lemnius is referring to a widespread belief in antiquity and the Renaissance, popularized by Pliny the Elder, that the breath or touch of a menstruating woman could dim mirrors and kill crops.</note> dims the luster of ivory and mirrors, dulls the edge of iron, chokes the crops, and the contagion of their breath destroys the sprouts of gardens; and not only does she affect anyone she meets, but she even deforms herself with spots and blemishes. By a similar reasoning, when eyes are corrupted by bleariness and **ophthalmia** <note>original: ὀφθαλμίᾳ; a general term for inflammatory eye diseases</note>, it happens that the eyes of another person are affected. This was expressed with a beautiful likeness by **Ovid** and **Juvenal**:

<margin>Satire 2.</margin>
> When eyes look upon the wounded, they themselves are wounded:
> And many things harm bodies by transition.
> Thus sheep, herds, cattle, the whole flock in the fields
> Falls by the scab and foul mange of a single one,
> And the grape takes its bluish color from the grape it sees.

However, men breathe **contagion** <term>contagio; here meaning a physical "taint" or "infection" transmitted through the air</term> upon other men most powerfully when they stand directly opposite one another; for if the breath turns at an angle, or if the flow happens to be carried to the right or the left, it does not bring so much harm, nor does it infect with so great a stain. <margin>A comparison.</margin> For just as transverse and slanted vision—as is common with those who **squint** <note>original: "petis"; refers to those with strabismus</note> and those who are **dim-sighted** <note>original: "lusciosis"; those with poor or nocturnal vision</note>—is somewhat blunted and dimmed: so too those things which emanate from the eyes and other parts of the body, if they are carried obliquely, happen to be blunted and dimmed, and bring less evil to those standing by.

I myself am accustomed to observe this very thing quite carefully when I assist patients affected by contagion, so much so that I always speak with them while turned away, never standing between the **fireplace** <note>original: "fumarium"; the smoke-vent or hearth. Physicians believed that standing in the draft between a patient and a vent would draw the patient's "effluvia" directly toward the doctor.</note> and the one lying in bed. This **efflux** and emanation, although it does not show itself to the eyes and is less perceptible to the sense of sight...

# ON THE SECRETS OF NATURE
<meta>catchword: mi-</meta>

Although the term "Nature" is broadly applied, and each person can devise secondary definitions according to their own judgment, they are all nonetheless traced back to one point. Thus, to **Physicians**:
*Nature* is a quality implanted and innate in things.
*Nature* is the mixture and temperament <note>original: *temperies*, referring to the specific balance of the bodily humors</note> of the four elements.
*Nature* is the force and inclination of each individual's mind.
To **Philosophers**:
*Nature* is the principle of motion and rest <note>This is a classic Aristotelian definition, suggesting that things move or stay still because of their internal nature.</note>.
*Nature* is the specific difference which gives form to each thing.
*Nature* is an effective force and cause, the preserver of things, inserted into the whole world.

<margin>The proper definition of Nature</margin>
Nature (to define the thing more properly) is the order and sequence of divine works, which obeys His power and His words and commands, and borrows its strength from Him.

Of all these descriptions, and as many as can be devised by eloquent men, the primary cause and origin flows from that eternal mind as if from a most fruitful fountain.

# ON MIRACLES. BOOK I.

Since a human being consists of and is fashioned from both body and soul, and the body itself is the soul's **instrument** through which it carries out its actions, who should not give the highest care and attention to both parts? Who would not desire that the health and safety of both be perfectly maintained? This is especially true since one cannot exist without the other, nor fulfill its functions and duties without hindrance. For, as the poet says:

*Thus does the one thing require the aid of the other, and they join together in friendship.*
<note>original: "Alterius sic Altera poscit opem res, & coniurat amicè." A quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica*, used here to describe the symbiotic relationship between the physical and the spiritual.</note>

Indeed, the body is for a time fragile and mortal; but because it is the vessel and receptacle of the soul and serves its needs, God has destined it also for eternity. Through the mystery of the resurrection, He willed it to share in the same gift: namely, immortality.

¶ *It is most natural to produce one's own likeness, and therefore humans ought to use this power reverently, as a divine gift and an ordinance of God.*

## BOOK I: ON MIRACLES

### [THE POWER OF IMAGINATION]

...the cause appears to me to lie in the silent imagination of the woman. For if she conceives anything in her mind, or fixes her eyes without blinking on whatever is before her and impresses it upon her mind, the infant usually represents those things on its outer surface. Thus, during embraces and kisses, if the woman directs her eyes and thoughts toward her husband’s face, or imagines someone else who is present, his likeness usually shines forth in the offspring. Such indeed is the force and power of the imaginative faculty <term>imaginaria facultas</term> <note>In early modern medicine, the "imaginative faculty" was believed to be a physical force that could literally "stamp" images from the mother's mind onto the soft body of the developing fetus.</note>, that when a woman gazes too fixedly at something, it works to produce something similar to what was seen. This is so much the case that various forms of things happen to be induced in the infant, and moles, freckles, stains, and warts are imprinted, which cannot easily be washed away or cleared.

Thus, the matrons of our own country <note>The author, Levinus Lemnius, was a Dutch physician; "our country" refers to the Netherlands/Low Countries.</note>, from the sight of a **hare**, give birth to infants with the upper lip split and divided into two parts <note>This explains the historical origin of the term "harelip" for a cleft lip, based on the folkloric belief that seeing a hare during pregnancy caused the deformity.</note>. For a similar reason, some are born with snub and upturned noses, a distorted mouth, unbecomingly protruding lips, and a deformed overall habit of the body, because the woman, at the time of conception and gestation, had her eyes and entire mind and thought fixed upon certain **monstrous sights**. 

The artisans of nature are accustomed to work such a thing in other living creatures as well, by placing various colors of objects before them at the very moment of conception. This was the stratagem and craft used by **Jacob**, to whom the name **Israel** was afterward given <note>A reference to Genesis 30:37–39, where Jacob placed peeled branches in front of Laban's flocks so they would conceive striped and spotted offspring.</note>...

Likeness is a consideration of the soul and mind, in which many chance factors are believed to hold power: sight, hearing, memory, and the images received and absorbed at the very moment of conception <term>sub ipso conceptu</term>. Even a sudden thought arising about anything is believed to shape the likeness and mix forms; from this, some children show the image <term>effigiem</term> of their grandfathers, others of their fathers, and many of their relatives. In contrast, the minds of other animals are generally immobile and stable, and are similar within each of their own kinds.

...nature is present in the seed, it is diffused and poured across into the offspring. Thus, according to the sentiment of Catullus:

> *Each follows the seeds of his own nature.* <note>original: "Naturæ sequitur semina quisque suæ." While attributed here to the Roman poet Catullus, this line was a common Renaissance proverb regarding the power of heredity.</note>

Since the seed flows from the most important parts of the body and contains within itself the nature and power of all the limbs, it follows that whatever defects have taken hold in any part are shared by the offspring as an hereditary right <term>hereditario iure</term> <note>A legal term used metaphorically to explain how biological traits are "willed" to the next generation.</note>. Thus, those who are tainted by elephantiasis <term>elephantiasi</term>—commonly called leprosy <term>lepra</term> <note>In the 16th century, "elephantiasis" and "lepra" were often used interchangeably for various disfiguring skin diseases.</note>—epilepsy, gout of the feet <term>podagra</term>, gout of the hands <term>chiragra</term>, and other contagious diseases, imbue their children with these same vices. And since the mother’s blood is the primary nourishment of the fetus and the secondary source of procreation, it often happens that children contract more corruption from the mother, whether you look at the condition of the body <term>habitum</term> or the habits of the mind. In this way, among us, women who are wicked, drunken, or dull-witted produce children exactly like themselves, sharing in their mother's vices. Therefore, since there are many things that hinder morality and the integrity of life, and no fewer things that dishonor the image and shape of the body, the greatest care must be taken lest anything occur that might deform the soul with depraved morals or the body with some monstrous <term>monstrosa</term> <note>In this context, "monstrous" refers to physical birth defects or "prodigies" of nature.</note> appearance. And since physical appearance and the elegance of form are pleasing and welcome to everyone, we must accurately observe those things which, through the progression of natural causes, either grant the favor of beauty or take it away.

<header>ON THE HIDDEN THINGS OF NATURE</header>
<note>original: "DE OCCVLT. NATVRAE." This is from the header of Levinus Lemnius’s *De Miraculis Occultis Naturae* (1559).</note>

These matters depend chiefly on the woman’s imagination <term>muliebri imaginatione</term> <note>The "theory of maternal impressions" was a long-held belief that a mother’s thoughts, fears, or the things she saw could physically alter her unborn child.</note> and on those things that happen to her from the outside. Therefore, every effort must be made so that nothing [unseemly] is presented before the eyes of that sex, and that no absurd thought creeps in which might cause some harm in the crafting and shaping of the fetus <term>fœtu</term>. For if some evil should attack from any source, or if some terror or trembling from a chance encounter should occur, all that emotion and consternation immediately settles upon the fetus. The natural spirits <term>spiritibus naturalib.</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, these were vital vapors that directed the body's growth and nutrition.</note> and the humors <term>humoribus</term> <note>The four primary fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> are turned toward it, and the entire maternal faculty becomes occupied in shaping such a thing.

Indeed, a vehement and fixed thought—while it violently moves the appearances of things and turns them over again and again—impresses upon the fetus the form and figure that the constant imagination revolves, and induces the shape of the thing that was thought of. For the internal spirits and the abundance of humors paint and form the image of the thing devised. 

Nor indeed is it by chance, or without cause, that some people possess an enormous body, a grim and unpleasant gaze, protruding and swollen cheeks, a distorted mouth, and an unseemly grin. These things occur because pregnant women conceived such ghosts and images <term>simulachra</term> in their thoughts and minds, or because their eyes were too intently fixed upon them. Thus, there is nothing I usually disapprove of more among more wanton young women <term>lasciuiore s mulierculas</term> than the fact that they [occupy] themselves with little dogs <term>catellis</term> and monkeys <term>simiisque</term>...

# ON MIRACLES. BOOK I.

...fant. This is something that generally tends to happen to boys, the sick, the elderly, and those of a melancholic temperament; however, the sight of monstrous things is less troublesome to them than it is to young women <term>mulierculis</term>. When such women are presented with images of this kind, they fashion and produce something similar within the womb <term>vterus</term>. For since all their powers and natural faculties <term>facultates naturales</term> <note>In the medical tradition of this period, these are the innate biological forces responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</note> are entirely devoted to forming and shaping the fetus <term>fœtus</term>, it happens that when a woman is struck by some fright, all the humors and spirits <note>The "humors" were bodily fluids (like blood and bile) and "spirits" were subtle vapors believed to carry life force; both were thought to respond instantly to emotions.</note> are driven downward and flow into the retreat of the womb.

When the imagination <term>imaginatio</term> of the thing she has seen—clinging and deeply fixed within her mind—is added to these forces, the very power which oversees the formation of the child models that form and appearance which she has conceived in her soul, and impresses it upon the fetus itself. Nor is it said without reason: **"Imagination creates the event."** <note>original: "Imaginatio facit casum." A common Renaissance proverb suggesting that a strong mental impression can cause a physical reality or "accident" to occur.</note> 

By a similar logic, if a shrew, a cat, a weasel, or some such creature unexpectedly jumps onto her body, or if strawberries, cornelian cherries, cherries, berries, or a grape seed falls upon any part of her, it happens that a mark is immediately imprinted, and the traces of that thing are impressed upon that limb. This occurs unless, by chance, at the very moment these things strike her body, the woman quickly wipes the limb and moves her hand to her back or some more distant part of her body. Once this is done, the harm is immediately turned away, or the mark is fixed to the part she touched, because her entire imagination and natural faculty have been diverted to that spot. <note>This describes a long-standing folk belief in "maternal impression," where a mother could supposedly "move" a potential birthmark to a less visible part of the child's body by touching her own hip or back during a moment of fright.</note>

# ON THE HIDDEN SECRETS OF NATURE
<meta>catchword: fa- (Elizabeth)</meta>

Although all things are deservedly credited to the Creator of the entire universe <note>original: "universitatis opifici"</note>, many things nonetheless occur through the natural course of events, proceeding in their own order and being carried along by an innate motion. movement on the sixtieth, and comes forth into the light in the seventh month. But if he received form on the thirty-fifth day, he gains movement on the seventieth, and receives the beginnings of birth in the eighth month. 
<margin>{</margin>If, however, he attained his legitimate form on the forty-fifth day, he moves on the ninetieth day, and achieves birth in the ninth month."

Since the soul performs its functions and duties through the body and carries that dwelling around with it—just as a snail <term>cochlea<gloss>a snail or its spiral shell</gloss></term> carries its attached shell—it usually happens for the most part that when the body is affected, the soul is also affected. Most people hold the opinion that human souls are of the same condition, and exist with the same dignity and excellence, and that there is no difference between the soul of a wise man and a fool or a wicked man, nor should any distinction be established; but they think that actions are only hindered by reason of the **organ** <term>organum|In the 16th century, "organ" referred to the physical instrument of the body, particularly the brain, through which the soul acts.</term>, and the faculties of the soul are performed defectively through some flaw in it.

I, however, out of no desire for dispute or contradiction, am persuaded that the matter is otherwise. For although I am not unaware that due to the severity of a disease, a wound inflicted on the head, or finally a fall and concussion of the affected **brain**, the **mind** becomes numbed and a forgetfulness of all things is induced; it does not follow, however, that the soul is equal in all people, or that all have been allotted an equal power of judging, or equal skill in **reasoning** and judging. For not every soul—no matter how accurately it has been cultivated, or how much strenuous effort happens to be applied—is equally capable of the arts, disciplines, and every kind of doctrine and erudition, nor with equal teachability and skill. -> # CONCERNING THE HIDDEN SECRETS OF NATURE # <-

<meta>catchword: sol- (likely "solvatur," meaning "is dissolved")</meta>

[They] altogether deny that the body is received into the same fate, or that it will exist in an equal condition, or that it will ever live again. But these people do not thoroughly examine the nature of man, nor the logic of the entire completed workmanship; nor do they fix their eyes upon Him who stood as the author of this light <note>Meaning the light of life or consciousness.</note> for man, and by whose power man attained the beginnings of his life. For since the soul and body, indivisibly connected to each other, constitute a human being, it is necessary that the whole human—that is, both the soul—attain immortality, and that the body, through the mystery of the resurrection, shall be a participant in the same gift.

For the logic of man's formation will not allow one part to reach the end for which it was destined without the other, nor that a "halved" human, or only one part, should achieve blessedness. It is therefore necessary, and the design of the created work demands, that the body shall one day live again, and, by right of <term>postliminy</term> <note>original: "postliminio". A legal term referring to the restoration of rights and status to someone returning from exile or captivity; here it refers to the body reclaiming its life and union with the soul.</note> being joined back together with the soul, it will share an equal condition with it, and be a partner in the same gift. For when God was intent on forming man, He said:

> "Let us make man in our image and likeness."

By these words, He did not designate only one part, but the whole human, who is forged from body and soul. For these two, united and glued together, make up the human; but when they are separated and torn apart, they [disrupt the nature of] man...

### BOOK I. ON MIRACLES ###

[the human person] happens to be dissolved, and to be deprived of the honor of this name <note>Meaning the name or status of being the "image of God."</note>. Therefore, it seems to me that reason demands that both parts attain the same end—namely, either **blessedness**, if life was spent innocently, or **damnation**, if lived wickedly. Nor indeed would it be consistent with reason for the body to fall away from that hope of happiness, since it endures the troubles of this age equally. 

For truly, for the sake of the **soul**, it is sometimes subjected to lashes and whips; it receives blows and tortures; it experiences pains, faces danger, and undergoes the risk of life, such that those powers of the soul—the *sensing* and the *growing* <note>original: "sentientem ac vegetantem". These refer to the "sensitive" and "vegetative" souls, Aristotelian terms for the biological functions of growth and sensory perception shared with animals and plants.</note>—which are common even to brute beasts, happen to be bruised and torn apart. For in thoughts, words, persuasions, opinions, and judgments, the body sometimes acquiesces to the soul at its own disadvantage; it obeys it, and shows itself to be a partner and servant in all things. Therefore, the body would not unjustly seem to be treated with injury if it did not enjoy the same benefit. 

The body is indeed the soul’s **instrument**, by which it completes its actions and carries out its functions; but the soul uses the animate and sensing body in a different way than a **craftsman** or **architect** uses a saw, a hammer, or an axe. <margin>An elegant comparison.</margin> For the individual limbs are most aptly distinguished for their own duties and can be adapted to many uses. Moreover, I see that this distinction can be established between the body and the soul, as that which exists between the **Sun**...

...and the **Moon**. For although the Moon borrows its light from the Sun, it is not entirely devoid of its own power. Indeed, it is carried by a specific motion of its own and completes its own circuit. It conceives its light from the Sun just as a **mirror** does, or as polished cauldrons and basins reflect the brightness of a torch placed opposite them. While it exhibits no light unless illuminated by the Sun, it cannot be considered idle or "off-duty," since it completes its monthly course and measures out its own path in the heavens without the Sun's assistance.

In the same way, while the **Soul** certainly supplies strength to the body, the body is not lacking its own innate faculties and natural powers—namely, the qualities of the **four humors** <note>The four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed in Renaissance medicine to govern the body's health and temperament.</note>, through which it is made capable of all its functions and suited to carry out whatever is required of it.

<margin>Eclipse.</margin>
and a loss of light when the earth stands in its way. The former occurs when the Sun runs along the ecliptic line at the same degree as the Moon, and the latter when they are in opposition. In this same manner, the **body** and the **soul** experience their own damages and failings; sometimes one part benefits the other, and sometimes one hinders the other. 

Therefore, since there is such a great consensus between them and so faithful a partnership—and since they exchange mutual labors for as long as they keep watch in this station of life—it is only fair that the body, having been renewed through the **resurrection**, should be made a participant in the same reward and be admitted into the same **citizenship** <note>original: "municipatum," a legal term for the rights and status of a citizen in a community.</note>. Having received His body and blood, we are united with Him, and we conceive a certain hope and confidence in the immense charity and mercy with which He did not hesitate to spend His life to redeem us. 

It is fitting to make use of this very monument <note>The author refers to the Sacrament as a "monumentum," a physical reminder or memorial.</note> both regularly and especially toward the end of life, when death is already imminent. This is done so that tranquility might take root in our souls and the greatest confidence in Him might dwell in our minds, <margin>The Eucharist.</margin> and so that we might continually give thanks <note>The word "Eucharist" literally means "thanksgiving."</note> to Him for the inestimable gift of His shed blood. By this gift, He removed from us every stain of sin, and—having shaken off the terror of death and overthrown the tyranny of the most cruel enemy—He claimed His captives for liberty. 

By this holy symbol, therefore, we are made certain that we have been grafted into Christ, united to Him, and joined by the closest bond of love. <margin>Hebrews 6</margin> The result is that, supported by a most certain hope as if by a walking-staff, we trust that we shall attain those things which faith has conceived and persuaded us of through the inspiration of the Spirit. From this faith, as if from a root, the branches of Charity sprout forth, bringing the most abundant **fruits** <note>The text cuts off at "fru-", completed by the catchword "ctus" as "fructus" (fruits).</note> of good works—

<margin>Psalm 129</margin>

### ¶ Whether a rational soul is instilled in prodigious and monstrous births, as well as in those born prematurely, and whether they will be participants in the future Resurrection; incidentally, from what cause monsters are produced. Chapter XV.

Whoever possesses a human form, and—having followed the order of birth established by our first parent—is procreated from both sexes in the proper reason and manner, even if they are monstrous in appearance or deformed in habit, they are endowed with the gift of a **rational soul** <term>rational soul: In the philosophy of the time, this was the highest level of soul, unique to humans, which provided the capacity for reason, intellect, and immortality.</term>. Once they have finished the course of this age, they shall be participants in the future resurrection.

However, those who display nothing of a human being, and are formed from the mixing of another living creature, and who exercise their actions differently than humans do: these will neither be immortal, nor honored with a renewed body. Thus, **Fauns**, **Satyrs**, **Lemures** <note>original: "Lemures." In Roman mythology, these were restless or malevolent spirits of the dead.</note>, **Centaurs**, **Screech-owls** <note>original: "Striges." Mythological owl-like creatures or hags said to suck the blood of infants.</note>, **Tritons**, **Sirens**, **Harpies**, and whatever other fables antiquity has devised, neither possess a rational soul, nor shall they obtain the benefit of resurrection. Indeed, among so many thousands of men, there are many with enormous bodies, or with a foul and horrifying appearance, a pig’s snout, or an unseemly gaping mouth: but all these, although they have deviated from the natural human form, are nonetheless counted among the number of humans.

<margin>Abortion.</margin>
<margin>Efflux.</margin>

Doctors, however, establish a distinction between an **Abortion** and an **Efflux**. An efflux occurs when, after a woman has first conceived for a few days and the matter is massed together, it flows out and slips away prematurely due to the smoothness and slipperiness of the womb. In this case, something unformed flows forth—a mere rudiment of a future fetus and a rough sketch of a work just begun—which perishes and is cast out, much like the seeds and fruit-buds that fall from a fruit-shedding tree. 

An **Abortion**, truly, usually demonstrates limbs that are exactly formed. ### ON THE HIDDEN THINGS OF NATURE
<meta>catchword: tua- (likely "tuatur" or "tuantur" — meaning to protect or observe)</meta>

...bring about many diseases. Likewise, the diseases of the body affect the mind through a mutual sympathy and by the law of their partnership. And although external objects and many outside causes may stir up turbulent movements in a person, the primary cause and origin resides in the heart, as well as in the <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> and the <term>spirits</term> <note>Subtle vapors thought to circulate through the body, acting as the bridge between the physical organs and the soul.</note>: if these are moderate and not tainted by any foreign quality, the soul seethes less, and the mind is somewhat more calm. 

Thus, if the blood is pure and clear, if there is a balanced <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific "mixture" or proportion of humors unique to an individual's constitution.</note> and the body is in unimpaired health, it happens that a person is more slowly provoked and less harassed by anger, fear, or a desire for revenge. Or, if they are shaken by some emotion—since no one is entirely <note>original: "ἀπαθὴς" (apathes) — a Stoic term for being "passionless" or unmoved by emotion.</note> and free from feelings—immediately, once reason and the judgment of the mind are called into counsel, all the fervor of the soul softens, and the agitation is stilled. 

Evidence of this can be taken from David <note>The biblical King David, noted for his restraint when cursed by Shimei.</note> and Pericles <note>The Athenian statesman famous for his "cool" headedness and oratorical restraint.</note>; when a certain wicked man insulted them and heaped abuse upon them, they responded to him not with hatred or revenge, but with an act of kindness <note>original: "humanitatis officio"</note>. ...stir up fumes in the nostrils. <margin>Hunger kindles the bile.</margin> But this agitation immediately softens and is calmed once food is offered. This is why those who are full flare up with anger less than those who are fasting: because the body, being moistened by food and drink, is less dried out, and since the innate heat is tempered, the body is less prone to conceiving anger. Indeed, the natural faculties are then occupied with digestion <term>concoction: the archaic medical term for the "cooking" or transformation of food into nutrients within the body through heat</term>, and the yellow bile, which usually boils over in those who have not eaten, is diluted by the ingested liquids. 

In the same way, cauldrons, skillets, and frying pans catch fire more easily and spread a heavier stench to the nostrils when the liquid or floating fat is consumed and scorched by excessive heat. Indeed, all things that are deprived of moisture or fat stick to the pots and release foul-smelling vapors, such that it is often said in a popular joke, "From the same pot, both boiled and roasted meat are drawn" <note>original: "Ex eadem olla elixa atque assa depromi." A proverbial way of describing a pot that has boiled dry, causing the food intended for boiling to burn or roast against the metal.</note>. 

Therefore, it seems to me that lean people, and those who possess a dry temperament <term>temperament: the specific balance of the four bodily humors that determines an individual’s physical and mental constitution</term>, act wisely by not remaining hungry for too long and by providing fuel for their innate heat. For the body is dried out by untimely and long-lasting hunger, which ravages the nourishing moisture—what they call the *radical moisture* <term>radical moisture: in Renaissance medicine, the vital, primordial fluid present from birth that acts as the "oil" for the lamp of life; its depletion was thought to cause aging and death</term>; a subject on which we have spoken elsewhere.

### ON MIRACLES. BOOK I.

Many physicians complain that descriptions of herbs are deceptive, and that their virtues <term>virtues: the inherent medicinal properties or healing powers of a plant</term> are ineffective and fleeting. They argue that many plants commonly encountered in the writings of the ancients, when compared to our own, respond poorly to their names and descriptions. Because of this, they contend that these herbs are different species entirely, even if they bear the same name in our current age. Thus, they believe our local hyssop, beans, cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphyllon," literally "five-leafed."</note>, valerian <note>original: "phu." A term used by ancient writers like Dioscorides to refer to valerian.</note>, cereal typha, mash, rye, and spelt <note>original: "olyram." An ancient type of hulled wheat, often identified as emmer.</note> are different things altogether, simply because they do not match the descriptions of the ancients in every detail.

For my part, while I do not wish to advocate for anyone or defend the errors of those who have utterly hallucinated <note>The author uses this strong term to describe those who are completely deluded or mistaken in their botanical identifications.</note> in the cataloging and knowledge of herbs, I also think some do not judge everything strictly enough by the rule of reason <term>rule of reason: literally "to the level" or "according to the plumb line," meaning with exact precision</term>. Although in such great variety and mutation of herbs, individual plants cannot always be categorized into a fixed class, nor is it easy to assign them a certain nomenclature matching the descriptions of the ancients, one should not think they are entirely different from what the ancients described, or completely alien to the medicinal effects they attributed to them. 

For nature itself provided the cause for this variety (if any exists); nature constantly changes its face and plays freely in bringing forth stocks and propagating seedlings, so that sometimes it seems to have produced something different from the parent plant. To this is added...

# ON THE HIDDEN MIRACLES OF NATURE

...[they] grow taller, and at other times more stunted. Some spring from the ground with many runners, while most emerge without any neighboring shrub or offshoot. Some, depending on the condition of the earth, possess a diluted and milky greenness, while others are saturated with a verdure verging toward a dark black. <margin>An analogy.</margin> For just as boys whose nurses withdraw their nourishment—or administer it too sparingly—become thin and wasted, taking on a bloodless and less healthy color; so too herbs born in lean, hungry, and thirsty soil become scaly and rough, appearing sad and unpleasant to the eye. 

From this, one can see herbs born among ruins and steep rocks that are scarcely nine inches <note>original: "dodrantem," a Roman measurement of three-quarters of a foot</note> high, yet these same plants, when committed to fertile and rested soil, exceed a cubit and a half <note>original: "sesquicubitum," approximately 27 inches</note> and spread their branches far and wide. Thus **bugloss** <note>a plant of the borage family, *Anchusa*</note> and **comfrey** (commonly called *Consolida maior* <note>Greater Comfrey</note>) are very often seen with small white flowers. Thus the **carnation** <note>original: "gariophyllæa," likely the clove pink or *Dianthus*</note>—either through the zeal of cultivation or the richness of the soil—displays white, red, or variegated flowers from the growth of a single stem and stalk. 

Thus the purple color of **violets** sometimes fades into a cornflower-blue or a pale sky-blue. By a similar logic, the leaves of some stalks are less notched and serrated, and "thorny-edged" <term>acanacra</term> <note>From the Greek *akantha* (thorn) and *akros* (at the end/edge)</note> plants—that is, those which bristle with thorns—become mild depending on the nature of the high or low ground where they grow, becoming less hostile with their spikes. ### ON THE SECRETS OF NATURE
<note>original: "DE OCCVLT. NATVRAE"</note>

<margin>*On the Causes of Plants* <note>Theophrastus’s *De causis plantarum*, a foundational work of botany</note></margin>
...I would believe that the efforts of cultivators either fail or fall into decline. Thus **wheat**, as Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> testifies, transforms into **darnel** <note>original: "lolium," a weed that looks like wheat but is actually toxic</note>, **basil** into **wild thyme**, and **water-mint** into **garden mint** in its scent, yet in its form it changes into **calamint**. Indeed, many kinds of flowers, unless care is applied and they are frequently transplanted, decline not only from their own species, but even from their innate strength and nobility. I am accustomed to observing this in many plants, but especially in the **cultivated violet**, a most esteemed flower; unless it learns to change its location every year, it fades into a lowly and degenerate little blossom, and becomes less fragrant. Virgil supports these observations:

<margin>*Georgics, Book 1*</margin>
> *I have seen seeds, though long chosen and tested with much labor,*

Conversely, if you apply care to wild and uncultivated plants, they soon grow mild, having shed their natural and innate wildness. Virgil expressed this beautifully:

> *Grafts them, or moves them to well-worked pits,*
> *Will shed their wild spirit, and by frequent cultivation*
> *Will follow whatever arts you call them to, and will not be slow to do so.*

<margin>Theophrastus, *On the Causes of Plants*, Book 1, Chapter 1</margin>
Thus, in sandy places—such as the sandy hills among the **Zeelanders** <note>People of the Dutch province of Zeeland</note> which the common people call **Dunes** <note>original: "Dunen"</note>—many shrubs spring up spontaneously from a convergence of nutrients; and because that location is exposed to the Sun and suited for producing herbs, once they are born from the dampness of the earth without a parent plant, they afterwards propagate themselves by seed and protect their kind with numerous offspring.

For this reason, no one should wonder that herbs are subject to mutations, and are subsequently deprived of their strength and form. This is caused by the site of the location, the quality of the surrounding air, and the skill of the cultivator (unless it happens that they are simply confused due to their affinity and similarity to other plants). Thus **pepper**, **cardamom**, **meadow saxifrage** <note>original: "seseli"</note>, and **rhubarb** <note>original: "radix Pontica," literally "Pontic root," a common name for rhubarb or sometimes liquorice in early herbals</note>, when accustomed to our climate, are changed somewhat; they do not possess such a hot and burning potency. Yet, no one would judge them to be anything other than what they truly are. The fact that their strength fades and they are denied their proper size and maturity is caused by the weak heat of the Sun and the intemperance and inclemency of the weather. Thus, herbs undergo a twofold mutation...

# ON THE OCCULT THINGS OF NATURE
<note>original: "DE OCCVLT. NATVRAE"</note>

It is established: for sometimes it happens that their implanted powers and native qualities are changed, while the form and appearance persist; at other times, the specific form perishes, while the very qualities and the power of their virtues remain. This is caused partly by the influence of the stars, partly by the nature of the soil, and by the quality of the surrounding atmosphere. Since the condition of the earth is varied and its differences are manifold, it happens that herbs are clearly changed by reason of both the air and the nutrients, and come to partake in a different quality. Thus the **Hazel**, **Cherry**, and **Cornel** tree, if they stand near banks where foul waters lap or salt waters wash and irrigate them, a clear saltiness <term>falsilago<gloss>a salty or brackish quality in the sap or fruit</gloss></term> is found to be present in the fruit. Similarly, humans—depending on the power of their food and the condition of the surrounding air—acquire a different bodily habit and temperament, as well as different morals and interests. Thus a **Cimbrian** <note>A member of a Germanic tribe, often used by Renaissance authors to represent Northern Europeans</note> transforms into a **Spaniard**, or a **German** into a **Gaul** or an **Italian**, through long-standing commerce and the practice and custom of life. Likewise, you may often see a joyful and shining tree, when moved to a salty and defective place, perish from the juice of the inferior earth.

# ON MIRACLES. BOOK I.

...fellow citizens. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a thought from the previous page regarding the duty of professionals toward their community.</note> However, as Cicero testifies, all arts are handled in one way by those who apply them to practice and compel them to serve human utility, and in another by those who, delighted by the study and theory of the arts—that is, by the love of speculation—intend to do nothing else in life but derive amusement and pleasure from them. For just as with virtue, all praise for any art consists in action. Since, therefore, the <term>medical art<gloss>original: "res medica"</gloss></term> demands such great diligence and requires tireless and restless labor, industry must never be interrupted; instead, the nature of diseases must be sharply explored, and a plan must be entered upon by which we may overcome their cruelty.

# ON THE HIDDEN THINGS OF NATURE
<meta>The header "DE OCCVLT. NATVRAE" refers to Levinus Lemnius’s famous work "De occultis naturae miraculis" (On the Hidden Miracles of Nature).</meta>

...[and] never show themselves to be diligent tillers of the soil. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a metaphor comparing the cultivation of the mind to the cultivation of a field.</note> I interpret this very same thing regarding the talents of our own men: the **parent of nature** <gloss>original: "naturae parens," a common Renaissance personification of Nature as a mother or creator.</gloss> has denied them nothing, nor did she grant everything to the ancients. Therefore, talent is not lacking in those who come after, provided that the mind is not lacking, and provided there is a ready and willing inclination to pursue the arts—so long as a similar passion and a desire for inquiry seizes them. This was a popular Renaissance maxim emphasizing that hard work and habit can overcome natural limitations.</note>

However, one can see that many are industrious, diligent, and eager to learn during their very **apprenticeship** <gloss>original: "tyrocinio," referring to the initial training period of a soldier or student.</gloss> in practicing their art. They perform their duties slackly and with too little attention; they become harsh, stubborn, intractable, unkind, and less dutiful than they were before. Driven by a certain <term>self-love<gloss>original: "philautia," a term derived from Greek meaning excessive self-centeredness or conceit.</gloss></term> and a hollow self-persuasion, they look down on others and are reluctant to allow a colleague or a partner in their labors to be joined with them.

Among these, there are also those who prematurely and precipitously rush into the practice of medicine. They are destitute of those supporting tools with which it is proper for a Physician to be equipped—things which they ought to have learned long ago, rather than learning them now. Thus, they obtain the title or the commendation of "Physician" before they have actually **earned it.** <note>The Latin text ends with "prome-", completed by the catchword "riti" to form "promeriti," meaning to deserve or earn through merit.</note>

### ¶ How varied and manifold is the nature and condition of the soil and earth. Chapter XVIII.

NOW indeed, to add something related to the previous argument, I believe that physicians should especially observe the nature of every land and the condition of the soil. For it is this that causes various species of herbs to emerge, and allows them to obtain diverse virtues and properties. <margin>In the Letter</margin> Hence Hippocrates instructs Crateuas <note>original: "Cratenæ." Crateuas was a famous Greek herbalist; Hippocrates’ correspondence with him, though likely apocryphal, was a standard reference for Renaissance botanists.</note> that mountain herbs, grown on high mounds, should be collected, since they are firmer, more robust, and more effective than aquatic ones, due to the density of the earth and the thinness of the air. However, he says their flowers should be gathered from those growing near springs, rivers, and streams, which he considers to be weaker, lacking much strength, and possessing a sweeter juice. 

Since, therefore, the power and <term>temperament</term> <note>Temperament: In early medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a plant or person.</note> of herbs are known from an exact consideration of the soil's nature—and since some herbs thrive in certain places and demand the earth most familiar to them—I shall mention their differences in passing, as if depicted on a map, so that each plant can be matched to its own place and be less deprived of its strength due to the poor quality of its nourishment and sap. These are the distinctions which Virgil pursues in part in his work. <margin>The 2nd Book of the *Georgics*</margin> <note>The *Georgics* is a famous poem by the Roman poet Virgil concerning agriculture and the relationship between humans and the land.</note> For it is for this reason that they do not respond to our wishes,

### ¶ Why Hesiod disapproved of manuring.
## Chapter XX.

Hesiod, a diligent writer on rural matters, is criticized by many because he neglected the manure pile in his works on agriculture. Yet he was not ignorant of the practice, but rather prioritized healthfulness over mere fertility. For he believed that sterility should be overcome with a different kind of enrichment <note>original: "laetamine." Literally "that which makes the land glad," used as a poetic term for fertilizer.</note> than the common use and habit of manuring. For he held that the stalks of lupines, chickpeas, peas, and beans, if overturned by the plow at the right time, or other fodder laid low, were enough to make a field rich and fertile...

<summary>Lemnius explains that plants grow and swell under the Moon's influence at night, much like the body recovers during sleep. He then begins a defense of Hesiod’s agricultural methods, favoring "green manure" (plowing under crops) over animal waste for healthier soil.</summary>
<keywords>Hesiod, Virgil, agriculture, manuring, plant growth, Moon, Sun, fertility, green manure</keywords>

# ON MIRACLES. BOOK I.

...he thought should be done. <note>Completing the thought from the previous page: Hesiod believed that natural enrichment through specific plants was the preferred way to achieve fertility.</note> For whatever products come from fields that have been manured and cultivated with dung provide faulty and less healthy juices. <note>original: "succos." In the science of the time, the "juices" or humors of a plant were thought to be directly transferred to the person eating them, affecting their health.</note> Thus, wheat and all cereal grains are more quickly infested by weevils <term>curculionibus: snout beetles known for destroying stored grain</term>, and the fruits and legumes of every kind grown in such fields can neither endure nor be preserved for very long without either contracting mold or being infested by borers <term>teredine: larvae that tunnel through wood or dried organic matter</term> and little worms. Even beer <note>original: "Zythus," a Greek-derived term often used for ancient or foreign styles of beer.</note>, and that drink which the Belgians call ale <term>Cereuisia: the standard Latin term for beer, distinguished here as a regional specialty</term>, when brewed from such crops, is spoiled very quickly and turns sour.

For this reason, in my opinion, Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet (c. 700 BCE) whose work "Works and Days" served as a foundational guide for ancient farming and morality.</note> was right to judge those fields as suitable and fit for sowing which are cleared by temperate winds and cherished by the sweet rays of the Sun—places where no water stagnates, and the soil is not made "fat" by the cultivation of manure, but rather achieves maturity through pure, native moisture and heat. For in this way, the things that grow there remain uncorrupted for a long time and provide a healthier form of nourishment. Indeed, it is impossible for long-lived people or those of perfect health to exist in regions where either the air itself or the food is faulty and prone to decay. The first of these conditions occurs where ponds and marshes exhale a heavy stench; the second occurs where the soil is fattened not by its own natural moisture, but by that which is added from the outside through the practice of manuring.

Thus, I have it proven by experience that the intestinal worms <term>lumbrici: typically large roundworms that inhabit the human gut</term> of children are driven out by the eating of raisins, if you offer them to those who are fasting, with no other food mixed in. For just as bitter things are hostile to worms, so too are sweet things when swallowed in abundance. For it happens that the worms are distended and burst by the plenty of the sweeter food. In this same way, the human stomach also swells and conceives griping pains <term>tormina: severe, twisting abdominal pains or colic</term> when sweet things are ingested in excess.

...they are accustomed to doing, whenever a man has remained fasting for a longer time. For then they inflict bites on the stomach and desire to be filled with food; and since nothing is offered to them by which they can be nourished and sustain their life, they are carried upward and hunt for food as far as the passage of the throat. For by a certain instinct of nature, they sense that nourishment slides down into the stomach <term>ventriculum: the stomach or belly</term> through those parts; and since the nostrils are open and face toward the path of the throat, they also take themselves there. Once a tickling sensation is produced, they are either ejected by a sneeze <note>original: "sternutamento"</note> or are pulled out, caught by the fingertips.

These things have often been observed by me in healthy people; once I had explained the cause of the occurrence to them, I made them feel at ease regarding this matter. Among the sick, however, I have seen this very thing happen occasionally, but not without the omen <note>original: "praesagio" — a foretelling or sign</note> of an approaching evil. For in such bodies, there is such contagion, such putrefaction, and such inflammation of the humors <term>humorum: the bodily fluids like blood and bile that doctors believed governed health</term> that the worms cannot endure the deadly force of the disease. Therefore, some burst forth to the outside, driven by the severity of the illness, rather than by a "crisis" <note>In ancient medicine, a "crisis" was the moment a disease was naturally expelled from the body</note> or by the force of nature. 

<margin>Book 2, Aphorism 18</margin>
However, when the violence of the disease is subsiding and it happens that they are washed out below with the rest of the excrement, Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> determined that this is a healthy sign. But to exit of their own accord, without any impulse of the natural faculty—as we see in those near death—is harmful to the bedridden. For they sense the [failing] of nature...
