In this way, it has been observed that shrews <term>sorices: specifically field mice or shrews</term> and dormice <term>glires: rodents known for hibernation</term> abandon ruinous houses, even as long as three months before they are set to collapse. Lice and fleas also, when they feel a human body wasting away <note>original: "tabescere"</note> and all the limbs being gradually deprived of blood, either desert the body entirely or occupy those parts where blood and natural heat linger longer. For it has been found by undertakers <term>Libitinariis: Roman officials in charge of funeral rites and the equipment for burials</term> and pallbearers <term>Vespillonibus: those who carried the corpses of the poor to burial, usually at night</term> that these insects hide themselves in that hollow around the opening of the stomach where the sword-shaped cartilage <term>cartilago ensiformis: the xiphoid process, the small cartilaginous extension at the lower part of the sternum</term> ends, or in the area beneath the chin which rests upon the vocal artery <note>likely referring to the carotid artery or the larynx area</note>. Inasmuch as those parts, being near the heart, remain warm until the final breath <note>original: "halitum"</note>. Since this had been reported to me by several people who attended to the sick, I unhesitatingly pronounced it to be a most certain proof of imminent death and an indubitable sign of a soul already departing. Furthermore, since we made mention of worms <note>original: "lumbricorum"</note> a little earlier, it seemed worthwhile to add this: that there are many things which expel and destroy worms and the internal contents of the belly. But nothing is more effective than [those things] dried on a roof-tile...

...much as when the throat is inflamed by worms, if that aforementioned powder <note>presumably made from the dried or burnt remains of the parasites mentioned previously</note> is administered to those suffering from infestation, it happens that the remaining worms clinging to the body are immediately cast out. 
<margin>Pliny, Book 10, chapter 25</margin>
This follows the same reasoning that Pliny and many other investigators of hidden matters <note>original: "rerum abditarum indagatores"</note> assert: that for a person struck by scorpions, a remedy is found in drinking the ashes of those very scorpions, dissolved in oil or wine. In the same way, our own countrymen testify that the bite of a rabid dog is cured by the burnt hairs of that same animal, when they are offered to the patient in wine. For this drives out the evil and renders the venom <term>virus: used here in the classical sense of a potent biological toxin or secretion</term> harmless, making it less hostile to the bitten body because it draws out the poison and neutralizes it. Thus, sometimes poisons of contrary power, when doubled and mixed together, serve as a remedy rather than a cause of death. The poet Ausonius indicates this in a witty epigram concerning a wife who wished to kill her husband with aconite <term>aconitum: a highly toxic flowering plant, also known as monkshood or wolfsbane</term>:

> *An adulterous wife gave poisons to her jealous husband,*
> *Yet she did not believe enough had been given to cause death.*
> *She mixed in lethal weights of quicksilver,* <term>argenti vivi: mercury; literally "living silver"</term>
> *So that the doubled force might compel a swift end.*
> *If one were to separate these, they act as distinct poisons:*
> *But he who drinks them joined together receives an antidote.* <note>original: "Toxica zelotypo dedit vxor mœcha marito... Antidotum ſumet qui ſociata bibet." This refers to the ancient belief that mercury and aconite could neutralize one another's toxicity.</note>

### ¶ *That Humors, not Evil Spirits, Bring on Diseases: yet Aerial Spirits Mingle Themselves with Them as if in Storms and Add Fuel to the Fire. Chapter I.*

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap 'N' in a square frame featuring a classical figure, possibly a scholar or deity, seated amidst architectural and foliage details.</image-desc>

THERE are many among us who, although they are only moderately trained in the works of nature, and are ignorant of the causes, origins, progressions, and the accompanying symptoms or accidents of diseases, and cannot grasp the logic behind them, attribute these very things to evil and hostile spirits <note>original: Genios; refers to "genii" or supernatural entities thought to influence human fate</note> who constantly watch over our misfortunes. Thus, they imagine that those who lie sick from a tertian fever <term>tertian fever: a fever that recurs every third day by inclusive counting, often associated with malaria</term>, are tormented by an evil spirit whenever the third day enters the veins; they imagine the same in a quartan fever <term>quartan fever: a fever recurring every fourth day</term>. They believe such a thing occurs in *Synochis* <note>original: Synochis; a medical term for a continuous fever that does not remit</note>—that is, continuous fevers—in daily fevers, in ephemeral or "one-day" fevers, and in all burning and scorching fevers. Otherwise, whatever is stored within them is spoiled and turns sour.

<margin>Book 2, Aphorism 10</margin>
In this regard, Hippocrates seems to me to have spoken most rightly: **The more you nourish impure bodies, the more you harm them.** <note>original: "Impura corpora quáto magis nutrias, tantò magis lædes." This famous medical maxim warns that giving rich food to a sick person whose body is "unclean" only provides "fuel" for the disease to grow worse.</note> For nourishment putrefies and is corrupted when mixed with faulty humors, and thus it happens that the patients struggle longer with their ailment. Or, if ever the disease begins to soften by the industry of the Physician or the forces of nature, it flares up again and is renewed upon the slightest occasion. 

Indeed, a new and recent corruption and rot is brought into the body, accompanied by a foul odor and stench—which we even perceive from the breath—which, being widely spread through the body, corrupts the **spirits** <term>spiritus; the "vital breaths" or subtle substances believed to animate the body and mind</term> and extinguishes the **innate heat** <term>calorem nativum; the fundamental internal warmth of a living being, considered the source of life and digestion</term>, because perspiration is inhibited.

<margin>Book 2, Aphorism 12</margin>
To this refers that opinion of Hippocrates: **If any traces or any remains stay behind in the body, relapsing diseases are stirred up, and fevers...**

### ON THE SECRET THINGS OF NATURE

[to be] rekindled. For nourishment taken into the body does not increase one’s strength, but is corrupted by the mixing of **foul juices** <term>praui succi; faulty or diseased humors</term>, and gives growth to the disease: this we observe in **quartan fevers** <note>original: "quartana"; a fever where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day, associated with black bile</note>, and in bastard or false **tertian fevers** <note>original: "tertianis"; a fever recurring every third day, associated with yellow bile</note>, when patients do not obey the Physician, nor observe a suitable dietary regimen.

<margin>
The cause of the intervals in fevers.
</margin>

Yet these fevers are intermittent and offer intervals of relief because the **humor** <term>humor; one of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</term> sits outside the veins and is farther from the heart. In continuous fevers, however, it happens that men are afflicted without ceasing, because of the sharp and stinging vapors of inflamed blood and ignited bile within the cavities and channels of the veins. Since these vapors have no free exit or ventilation, they strike the heart and liver directly; and because of the **putrefaction** <note>original: "putredine"; the "rotting" or breakdown of humors which was believed to cause the heat of a fever</note> arising from **blockage** <term>oppilatione; a Renaissance medical term for an obstruction in the vessels or organs</term>, they infest the body more mercilessly than if they were poured out outside the veins. Indeed, since there is a great abundance of humors and violent putrefaction, and a great tendency of this humor toward decaying (for blood, by its quality of heat and moisture, more readily catches putrefaction), it follows that these fevers rage continuously and hasten very quickly to their peak.

<margin>
Book 2, Aphorism 23.
</margin>

Whence **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) whose writings formed the foundation of Western medicine</note> asserts that diseases are not extended beyond the fourteenth day: but sometimes, where the matter is fierce and swells up, they are terminated on the fifth, seventh, ninth, or eleventh day. # ON MARVELS. BOOK II.

[...to be] rekindled. The causes of **fevers** <term>febrium; illnesses characterized by increased body heat, then believed to be caused by rotting humors</term> which invade through cycles and fixed intervals arise from a certain power and quality innate to the **humor** <term>humor; one of the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that governed health</term>, as well as from the logic of the specific location and time. These factors determine why they attack intermittently: why they **anticipate** <note>original: "anticipent"; meaning the fever attack begins earlier than the previous cycle</note> their onset, why they move more sluggishly or later, why they are unstable and inconsistent, or why the **paroxysm** <term>paroxismus; the period of a fever's greatest intensity</term> is protracted for a longer duration.

<margin>
Anticipating.
</margin>
These attacks are anticipated and grow stronger when it happens that the humor increases and is more ardently inflamed, or where some error in lifestyle has been committed, or when there is some intemperance in food and drink.

<margin>
Delaying.
</margin>
But the fever invades more hesitantly and later, and the assault grows mild, when the matter of the disease is diminished; once the **blockage** <term>oppilatione; a Renaissance term for an internal obstruction or "clogging" of the vessels</term> and the **putrefaction** <note>original: "putredine"; the "rotting" of humors believed to generate feverish heat</note> are dispersed, the obstruction is gradually calmed and settles down.

<margin>
Unstable and wandering.
</margin>
When, however, one humor takes on the nature of another, or changes its location, or is confounded by mixing with another, the cycles proceed with no order and with unstable movement; they do not observe any certain or predictable manner of onset.

<margin>
Long attacks.
</margin>
A long-lasting attack is caused by humor and vapor that is copious, spread widely through the body, and is ultimately thick and viscous.

<margin>
A simile.
</margin>
Just as damp and green wood cannot be ignited and consumed except over a long period, and just as beef—especially when it is old and aged—requires long boiling to be prepared, so must a viscous humor be macerated longer and softened by **concoction** <term>concoctione; the internal "cooking" or ripening of humors by the body's heat</term>. It must become fluid so that it may be rendered suitable for **excretion** <term>excretioni; the process of the body discharging waste or "corrupt" humors</term>.

### ON THE HIDDEN WONDERS OF NATURE

<margin>
Intermittent fevers.
</margin>
Furthermore, as it was demonstrated a little while ago, when **humors** <term>humores; the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to dictate health and temperament</term> rot outside the veins and are inflamed in any part of the body, they stir up intermittent fevers, which grant the patient certain intervals of "breathing space" or relief. However, we frequently observe these same humors inciting continuous movements—even when they are located outside the veins—on account of both their sheer volume and their ferocity. This very phenomenon can be seen in parts of the body seized by **inflammation** <note>original Greek: "φλεγμονῇ" (phlegmonē); a localized heat and swelling</note>, in a **Carbuncle** <term>carbunculo; a severe, painful cluster of boils often associated with infection</term>, in **buboes** <term>bubonibus; the tell-tale swollen lymph nodes of the bubonic plague</term>, and in every contagious and pestilential **abscess** <note>original: "apostemate"; a collection of infected matter</note>. In these cases, the fever that is kindled is not intermittent, but continuous, even though the poison has erupted outside the veins and is located further from the heart. For this pestilential and poisonous force penetrates to the heart itself, attacking the "principal parts" of the body and infecting both the **natural and vital spirits** <term>spiritus; the subtle vapors or "breaths" believed to circulate through the organs to sustain life and function</term>. Because of this, such diseases are classified among the "acute" illnesses, because they hasten rapidly toward their **crisis** <note>original: "statum"; the turning point of a disease</note>,

### BOOK II.

...whom one can recognize from their eyes, their facial expression, their gait, their clothing, and the whole condition of their body. They arrange and alter each of these in various ways, frequently taking on another persona—like that of an actor, a wrestler, or even a charlatan <term>agyrtha; a traveling street-performer or quack who gathers a crowd for trivial entertainment</term>. This leads them to leap up in their sleep and create a commotion of applause and noise, driven by the mental images <term>simulachra; phantoms or likenesses of real things</term> that strike their senses and match their daytime desires and actions. 

In this way, when any of us is intensely focused on a task or dealing with serious matters during the day, the appearances and ghosts <note>original: "species ac spectra"</note> of those things occupy the mind at night and wring out loud and turbulent cries. > *In dreams, we mostly see ourselves engaged in the same things:*

For those things which are accustomed to exhaust and press upon us all day long leap into the brain as the day wanes. They stir up nocturnal disturbances, or at least keep the mind occupied and trapped by them, so that sleep is not peaceful but is repeatedly interrupted by the images presented to it.

### ¶ *Regarding those who have drowned: the corpses of men float on their backs, but those of women float face down; and they do not resurface if the lungs are removed. Chapter VI.*

<margin>Pliny, Book 7, chapter 17.</margin>
It has been discovered among the Belgians—a fact which Pliny also confirms—that the bodies of men, when they have drowned, float on their backs <note>original: "supina"</note> with their faces turned upward toward the sky. The bodies of women, however, float face down <note>original: "prona"</note> with their countenances tilted toward the bottom. It is believed that by this, Nature looked out for the modesty of the sex, so that those parts which are more decently covered would not come into view or be displayed to the eyes of men <note>This "modesty of nature" was a common teleological explanation in Renaissance science, suggesting that the natural world followed human moral codes.</note>.

However, the reason I have devised is that a woman is more "bellied" <note>original: "ventricosa"</note> and possesses a larger womb with wider cavities, a belly, intestines, urinary passages, and spongy, swollen breasts. Since these are filled abundantly and flowingly with fluid, it happens that the belly is weighed down by the weight and the distension of the waters and is carried downward. We see this very thing in sealed skins <term>utriculis; small leather bags or wine-skins used as containers</term> and vessels: the part containing air stays high, while the part containing fluid sinks and rolls downward. One may observe the same thing in an egg cast into brine: it floats, certainly, but the part where the weight resides is pressed down and sinks, while the part filled with air—namely that which shows a hollow when the shell is broken—stands out and rises above the surface when the eggs are quite old and starting to spoil <note>original: "subolida"; refers to eggs that are slightly turned or stale, which develop larger air pockets and thus float differently.</note>, sur-

...[on their back,] while women float on their belly. For it is so arranged by nature that every heavy thing is carried downward, while the light is carried upward. 

<margin>Those who have drowned do not emerge immediately</margin>
To this cause I also believe we should attribute the fact that those suffocated by water do not emerge immediately. For since it happens that the body is filled everywhere with moisture and weighed down by the weight of the water, it cannot struggle upward, especially since it contains no air within it, and all the breath <note>original: "spiritus"</note> has been forced out through the swirling water and has vanished. Truly, within the space of seven or nine days, the body dissolves, breaks apart, and decays, and the lung conceives a great deal of air. 

And hence it is that our common folk are accustomed to say repeatedly that on the ninth day, the body will emerge because the gallbladder has burst. This is not because the sac of the gallbladder is actually broken, but because the humors flow out from it and the other moist receptacles that have become flaccid from the soaking water. 

Whereby it happens that the body, its flesh having been thinned, becomes fluid, and the lung—which is porous like a sponge—takes in a great deal of air. This draws the corpse up and restores it to the breeze. For indeed, this organ supports and balances those floating in the water; the larger and more perforated and complex a person’s lungs are, the longer they can hold their breath and remain at the bottom for a longer time. 

I heard Master Vesalius <note>Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) was a pioneering Renaissance anatomist and physician to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>, a man of excellent talent and the highest erudition, relating a story in this way about a certain Moorish <term>diver; original "vrinatorem," a Latin term for a specialized diver capable of staying underwater for long periods</term>...

A certain absurd belief has taken root, and it deceives not only the ignorant and unrefined common people, but even some physicians of great reputation and primary fame: that many infants come forth into the light—not without some omen of good or evil fortune—with their heads covered by a "helmet" <note>original: "galea," referring to a caul, a portion of the amniotic sac that sometimes covers a baby's head at birth, long considered a sign of good luck or psychic ability</note>. They believe this because they are ignorant of the fact that this is common to all, and that the fetus is protected in the womb by these very membranes. Indeed, there are three coverings or membranes by which the fetus is protected in the hidden recesses of the mother's womb. The outermost is called **chorion** in Greek and the **Secundina** <note>The "second" or afterbirth</note> in Latin, because it emerges immediately after the birth. 

Beneath this lie two other membranes. The first of these is called the **Allantoides** <note>literally "sausage-shaped" in Greek</note> from its shape; it is generated from the female seed <note>The author reflects the 16th-century Galenic view that both parents contribute "seed" to conception</note> and is stretched over the head, buttocks, and feet, resting upon the protruding parts. Its purpose is to receive the urine of the formed infant. The last is a very thin membrane and skin which absorbs the sweat and vapor emanating from the maturing fetus, encircling and embracing it in a ring; it is called the **Amnios**, named for its lamb-like softness and tenderness <note>The author derives "amnios" from the Greek word *amnos*, meaning lamb</note>. Provident nature devised and fashioned these fortifications and protections for gestation so that the infant suffers no discomfort from rubbing, and to prevent it from being bruised. Sometimes the last of these membranes bursts forth with the infant, [clinging] to the parts...

Whenever the people of Lower Germany <note>Referring to the inhabitants of the Low Countries, such as the Dutch and Flemish</note> describe someone of an unsteady brain, or of an alienated and disturbed mind—one who appears similar to a madman in his habits, gestures, words, deeds, and in every action of life—they frequently say that he is "wandering in the beans." This is usually applied to men of a vacillating brain and those who lack the judgment of reason and mind. Thus Strabo <note>A Greek geographer (c. 64 BC–24 AD)</note> reports that among the <term>Sabaeans</term> <note>Ancient people of Southern Arabia (modern Yemen), famous for their abundance of frankincense and myrrh</note>, who were sometimes stunned into a stupor by the intensity of sweet odors, they were revived by the smoke of bitumen and the scent of a burnt goat's beard. Immediately, someone nearby brought to his nostrils some horse manure that was still warm and steaming (for he was accustomed to that smell) and thus restored his life.

In recent years, a remedy for the plague was employed when a common disease raged cruelly among the Nervii <note>A Belgic tribe of northern Gaul</note>—whom they now call the people of Tournai—and spread through the entire city. Indeed, the garrisoned soldiers who kept watch in the citadel turned their engines of war and <term>bombards</term> <note>Early large-caliber cannons</note> toward the city, filled with <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "puluere bombardico"</note> but no cannonballs. For this remedy is no less immediate in dissipating mists and the contagions of infected air than that which we read <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity</note> used to do: stirring up fires at the crossroads by building pyres and heaps of brushwood and bundles of sticks.

### ¶ *Certain things do not catch fire and are unconquered by flames. And by what means they achieve this. Chapter XII.*

We have seen finished and woven napkins made from a certain kind of **incombustible flax** <note>original: "lini quodam genere incombustibili"; this refers to asbestos, which was often called "mountain flax" or "salamander’s wool" in the Renaissance</note>, which do not yield to fire and are untamed by flames. This kind grows in the deserts of **India**, and in parched places scorched by the Sun, where certain plants, by the condition of the soil and the quality of the surrounding air, acquire that nature by which they can be fashioned and woven into linens. <margin>Book 9, chapter 33.</margin> For if in the sea and its currents <term>ostracoderma</term> <note>original: "ostracoderma," from Greek, meaning "shell-skinned"</note>—that is, creatures with a shelly skin—can grow solid, such as crabs, hermit crabs, lobsters, crayfish, whelks, scallops, and many kinds of shellfish, in which (as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" was the primary source for such wonders</note> says) there is a great variety of playful nature, and many differences of shapes and colors; if, finally, the shrub of **Coral** puts forth leaves at the bottom of the **Ligurian Sea**, and [is hardened] by the sea...

### ON WONDERS. BOOK II. ###

Doorposts, doors, and paneled ceilings <note>original: "lacunaria"</note> can be imbued with a green color, provided that a harder crust is spread over them, and alum and the ashes of white lead <note>original: "plumbique albi cineres"; referring to tin or lead-based pigments</note> are mixed copiously with the pigments. For the fiery force cannot penetrate them because the wood becomes compressed and dense, hardening against both fire and rain. 

A proof of this matter was given by **Archelaus**, the general of **Mithridates**, in a wooden tower. When **Sulla** attempted to set it on fire, he achieved nothing and was forced to depart with the task unfinished, desisting from the undertaking because everything had been smeared with alum, which is a powerful astringent. 

<margin>
Book 35,
chapter 15.
</margin>
Likewise, the effort of **Gaius Caesar** was in vain when, near the Po River, he brought fire to a fortress constructed from **Larch** wood. For the **Larch** tree, being similar to the **Spruce** <note>original: "Piceæ"</note>, neither catches fire nor sustains a flame. It is not only immune to rot and woodworms, but it does not even dissolve into coals or crumble into ashes because of a solidity and hardness exceeding that of horn, which the force of fire cannot penetrate or tame. 

<margin>
Larch
</margin>
Finally, it is of such weight that it does not float, but immediately settles and sinks, in the manner of **Boxwood** and **Ebony**. One might not undeservedly wonder why it does not burn and catch fire, given that it pours forth a resin of a honey-like color.

In former years, these diseases tortured and tormented men in unbearable ways; now they have begun to grow milder and are less aggressive. This has happened partly because, through the work of physicians, the force of the evil has been tamed and the cruelty of the humors <term>humors: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to determine health</term> has been mitigated. It is also partly because nature, through long habit, has grown callous to the pain. 

Thus, I have observed some who, in the flowering and fervent years of their youth, were most sharply tortured, yet the same individuals were more mildly afflicted as they grew old and their lives declined. For either the heat and boiling of the blood cools down, and the gathering of the humors becomes less, or else nature—having become accustomed to the evil over a long span of time as if it were a domestic and familiar thing—no longer struggles against it. For the body is either nourished by those corrupt humors, or it is no longer offended by them. <margin>A comparison.</margin> For just as swine, when they wallow in filth, or common laborers <note>original: *cerdones*; specifically low-class craftsmen like tanners or cobblers who worked with smelly materials</note>, or those who clean out public sewers and privies, do not notice the stench, so too those filled with disease <note>original: *morbillosi*; here referring generally to those pock-marked or chronically ill</note> are fattened by their own impurities. And because they have grown callous to the vices and diseases of the body (not to mention those of the soul), they no longer perceive the damage done to their nature—

### ->**The reason why those near death, even while their mind is still sound, produce a hoarse murmuring and a recurring sound, which the Belgians in the common tongue call "the rattle."** <note>original: *Den rotel*</note> **Chapter XV.**<-

In the region of Belgium, and throughout the whole stretch of the northern lands, those about to die offer certain signs of their departure by making a murmuring sound; indeed, there is hardly anyone who does not end their life without this kind of indication. For as death looms, they produce a sound like the murmur of water flowing through rough patches and winding, curved places, or like the sound produced by small pipes and tubes in aqueducts. For when the windpipe <term>vocalem arteriam: literally "vocal artery," the term used at the time for the trachea</term> happens to be obstructed, the breath <term>spiritus: the "vital spirit" or air believed to carry life through the body</term> which longs to burst out all at once, having found a narrow passage and a collapsed pipe, comes forth with a certain gurgling <note>original: *gagarismo*</note> and produces a hoarse murmur through the smooth parts, leaving the parched limbs like bubbling springs. Thus the gathered breath, mixed with swollen foam, rouses a sound similar to the ebbing and flowing tide of the sea. This very thing also occurs in some people because of the small tissues and membranes being contracted into wrinkles, so that the breath runs down in an oblique and winding path.

Indeed, the whole of creation, for man's sake, has been subjected to vanity and corruption: and the entire order and succession of things, even the angelic minds, long for a limit to be set to their labors. However, for those placed in such great calamity and misery, it is a consolation—and it lifts our spirits—to have the most certain hope of another life and the highest confidence in Christ, who restores the collapsed nature of man, returns it to its former integrity, and removes the trembling and fear of death from our souls. For the remembrance of his death and resurrection firmly supports us, which brings it about that we believe man is not destroyed, but changed for the better, and that death is not annihilation, but the vestibule <note>original: "vestibulum," an entrance hall or porch.</note> and doorway to another life.

# ON THE HIDDEN SECRETS OF NATURE.

<meta>catchword: ¶ Other</meta>

...and the most powerful remedy for restoring one’s strength. For liquids refresh those who are exhausted most rapidly; though they may not provide the same level of nourishment as solid foods, they far surpass them in how quickly they are distributed throughout the body. For this reason, the opinion of Cornelius Celsus <note>A famous Roman encyclopedist and medical writer from the 1st century AD.</note>—which does not contradict Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" from ancient Greece.</note>—is most true: 

<margin>Book 1.</margin> 
*When it comes to food, excessive fullness is never beneficial, and excessive abstinence is often harmful. Yet if any lack of moderation occurs, it is more severe in drinking than in eating.* 

By this, he indicates that more harm and damage is inflicted upon the body by the immoderate drinking of wine than by the gluttony <note>original: *ingluvie*; literally a bird's crop, but used here to describe ravenous or excessive eating.</note> of food. This is because drink immediately penetrates all the body’s passages; it enters the veins while still "uncooked" <note>meaning it has not yet undergone the slow, transformative process of digestion in the stomach.</note> and attacks the nerves and the brain. Food, however, remains in the stomach while it is being digested; if it becomes a burden, it is expelled through vomiting with very little effort. Nature finds this task far less easy or natural when dealing with liquid. 

This is proven by the fact that dogs, cats, dormice, and shrews, if they happen to swallow morsels or scraps tainted with poison, can vomit them up without trouble once the natural faculty for excretion is triggered. This is extremely difficult to achieve with liquids. Consequently, poisons administered in a drink are far more lethal than those in solid food. The venom <note>original: *virus*; used here in the general sense of a potent poison or toxin.</note> is swept most rapidly into every part of the body, corrupting and destroying the vital organs—especially if it is served in wine.

<summary>The author argues that while liquids restore strength faster than solids, liquid excess is more dangerous because it reaches the brain and nerves instantly. He also notes that poisoned drinks are more deadly than poisoned food because they are harder to expel and circulate faster.</summary>

ON MIRACLES. BOOK II. 134

# *¶ Wine intoxicates by a different power and method, and affects men differently than "Sicera" <note>A term used for any fermented intoxicating drink that is not grape-wine, such as cider or mead.</note> or "Zythus," which we call Beer. Chapter 19.*

<margin>How the nerves are produced from the brain.</margin>
Although the brain is soft and moist by nature, the nerves are produced from it just as webs and filaments are produced from a distaff <note>A tool used in spinning to hold the unspun fibers of wool or flax.</note> to which downy fluff and flax are attached. The connections of these nerves are distributed into all parts of the body. Indeed, from this principle and source, the nerves are derived into every limb, just as the offspring and progeny of branches spread out into many buds from the trunk and stem of a tree. The entire body perceives sensation and motion through them; when these are affected and the "ruling part" <note>The brain, considered the seat of the soul and the director of the body.</note> is harmed, the body is deprived of those functions or performs its tasks and duties weakly. However, while this condition arises from a weakness of the spermatic vessels, another kind of defect is contracted from the "embrace of Venus" <note>A common Renaissance euphemism for sexual intercourse</note> and contagious cohabitation, whenever men enter into congress with infected prostitutes. In such cases, a certain purulent and foul filth drips from the groin, sometimes bluish-black in color, sometimes the color of copper-rust or leek-green, and never without a most terrible stench.

### ¶ *That in diseases bodies grow and are extended in length, even though they eat less, but are diminished in width. Chapter XXIV.*

Daily experience proves that children below the age of puberty who consume a great deal of nourishment grow up less beautifully, nor are they drawn out to a proper and decent length. For the native heat <note>The "vital spark" or internal flame that Renaissance medicine believed drove digestion and growth.</note> is suffocated and overwhelmed by immoderate moisture, preventing the bodies from being shaped into a graceful height <term>proceritas</term>.

However, those who are fed moderately, use food more sparingly, and establish distinct and fixed times for eating, do not become greatly obese; neither fat nor flesh increases excessively in them, but the bones receive length and growth. Thus we see adolescents and boys in long and chronic illnesses grow thin and become gaunt <term>macilentos</term>, yet their bodies are extended in length and attain a great height.

...during the summer months to take a midday nap; nor do I think it advisable to indulge in sleep immediately after a vein has been cut <note>Original: *incisa vena*. The surgical opening of a vein for bloodletting.</note>, especially if someone has a full stomach or an obese body. For there are some among these people who, once the vein is pierced and blood removed, persuade themselves that their strength must be restored, and so they indulge their appetite <note>Original: *Genio indulgent*, a classical idiom meaning to feast or satisfy one's desires and pleasures.</note> abundantly. When they then become sleepy and start yawning, they give themselves over to rest—not without serious harm and the loss of their health. 

For indeed, the brain becomes filled with thick and dense vapors, and the veins usually swell so much that the incision gapes open, and the blood flows out again to the great detriment of one's health.

<margin>An example of one who was lulled into death by sleep.</margin>

I remember this happening here to a certain prominent man. On the Ides of May <note>May 15th.</note>, a day when three days of holidays and public prayers <term>supplicationes</term> <note>Solemn religious processions or days of communal petition to God.</note> were proclaimed, he had a vein cut. At lunch that day, he filled himself abundantly with wine and green garlic—as is the custom—and from midday, with his head filled with fumes, he was first lulled by sleep, and was afterwards overcome and silenced by death. 

For this reason, anyone who wishes to best look after their health should, on the day a vein is cut, establish a regime of frugal living and, as much as possible, restrain themselves from sleep. But if sleep should creep up even on the unwilling, and the eyes begin to blink, and the drowsiness cannot be shaken off entirely: nevertheless, let it be delayed at least until the rush and agitation of the blood has subsided—which occurs after the space of an hour and a half <note>Original: *sesquihoræ*.</note>.

...forth outwardly, or offers an argument for divination <note>The author refers to physiognomy, the practice of using physical features to "divine" or predict a person's character.</note>. For this reason, no one should be insulted on account of any physical defects. There are many who believe it is healthy to take one's sleep with a wide and open mouth; they argue that in this way, "fumes" <note>In early medicine, "fumes" or vapors were thought to rise from the stomach to the head during digestion.</note> are better exhaled, "soot" <note>original: *fuligines*. <margin>A comparison to a besieged city.</margin>
For something similar happens to those bodies as happens to a city oppressed by a very tight siege; since it is not sufficiently equipped with provisions and other defenses to repel enemies, it cannot endure even the slightest assault, but after one or two attacks, it wavers and falls into the power of the enemy. And just as an assault is sometimes interrupted, allowing for a brief breathing space, only to have the fight become more raw and intense again with renewed strength: so it happens in **acute diseases**, in which we observe the onset of the disease—like storms and violent winds—fall quiet, but then be renewed with such violence that nature can hardly endure, nor does it seem that life can be extended even to the seventh day.

### ON MIRACLES. BOOK II. 157

...it sharpens and restores tired eyes, for the <term>visual spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus visorij"; in early modern physiology, these were believed to be subtle, vapor-like substances that traveled from the brain through the optic nerves to enable the act of seeing.</note> are gathered together and are refreshed by new ones springing back from the brain. 

However, the reason why a mirror reflects an image from the opposite side has been a matter of doubt for many. Some indeed believe that there are **likenesses** <note>original: "simulachra"; a reference to the Epicurean theory that objects continuously shed thin, film-like layers of themselves that travel through the air.</note> in this—that is, figures of our bodies emitted from our own bodies. Others believe that images are not in the mirror itself, but that the bodies are seen when the line of sight of the eyes is twisted back and bent back upon itself. Thus, mirrors show things by means of reflected rays. 

Reflection occurs because of a dense object; for that reason, mirrors are coated on the back with lead, so that light is not transmitted directly through the glass. An object appears to be opposite because that part of the ray moving the eye is directed toward the opposite side; therefore, the whole ray is received as if it were stretched out in that direction, with the result that the object is displayed to the eyes. 

Furthermore, mirrors return images of the front part of the body, not the back, because the <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; in historical optics, this refers to the "sensible form" or image-likeness that flows from an object through a medium (like air) to the eye.</note> which flows from a solid body through the air to the surface of the mirror is simple and pure. Therefore, images shine in the mirror when luminous rays are thrown back from it: for, having been struck back, they spring back to the eye, in which each person beholds themselves and gazes upon a figure clearly expressed. For we do not see *through* the mirror, nor is the image formed *in* the mirror, but rather in the eye, although the mirror assists the process.

<margin>A comparison from seals.</margin>
For something similar happens with tablets or masses of wax or clay: if you press a seal into them and strike it in reflection, the parts display themselves in a contrary way. We perceive this same thing in typographic forms <note>A reference to the then-recent technology of the printing press.</note>, as well as in skillfully engraved plates, through which we see artistic <term>monochrome prints</term> <note>original: "monocromata"; here referring to images created without paint or pigments, such as woodcuts or copperplate engravings.</note>—that is, images delineated without any pigment or the deceit of colors—being expressed, in which the right parts always correspond to the left.

Furthermore, the reason why it happens that the Sun is seen doubled in a mirror placed under water (which also occurs in the clouds, as a <term>portentous omen</term> <note>The appearance of "mock suns" or parhelia was often interpreted in the Renaissance as a supernatural warning or sign of coming change.</note>, as some unlearned people think) has not been noticed by most. For there are those who think that the <term>Dog Star</term> <note>original: "caniculam"; Sirius, the brightest star in the sky.</note>, or some other star positioned nearby, is being seen, even though the brightness of the Sun so obscures all stars and planets that they cannot be seen during the day. 

In truth, a double image of the sun is displayed: first by the nature of the water, and then by the nature of the mirror. Indeed, that water expresses the nature of a mirror and makes everything look larger is testified to—besides common experience—by that famous Corydon of Virgil, <note>A character from Virgil's *Eclogues* who observes his reflection in the calm sea.</note>

->“Nor am I so ugly; I saw myself recently on the shore,<br/>

Firstly, then, the brightness of a mirror displays the form of the Sun through reflection; next, water does the same, as it happens that the Sun's rays are thrown back from its surface. The reasoning is the same for a torch, a candle, or the Moon when positioned opposite a mirror submerged in water, which displays a double image of the object through reflection. There are also <term>Burning Mirrors</term> <note>original: "vrentia specula"; concave mirrors designed to focus sunlight into a single intense point.</note> devised for another purpose: these are concave mirrors which, when placed facing the Sun, draw out fire and flames through reflection, and ignite straw, stalks, and other dry kindling and fuel. Thus we read that Archimedes <note>The famous Greek mathematician of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), who reportedly used mirrors to set fire to Roman ships.</note> burned the enemies' <term>triremes</term> <note>original: "triremes"; ancient warships with three banks of oars.</note> using burning mirrors. Indeed, in those mirrors, all the solar rays are reflected away from the point of impact and, converging at a single point, they set fire to whatever is in their way.

<margin>The kinship of molten lead with quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"</note>.</margin>
Molten lead emulates the condition of this silvery and most lively liquid <note>mercury</note> to some extent. Indeed, all things float upon it: iron, flint-stones, shells, and most other things that do not melt in fire, even though they are fluid and flowing by nature. For while nothing is hotter than liquid lead, gold, silver, and tin do indeed float upon it, but they immediately melt away and dissolve like wax. 

In this way, it is also related to **Quicksilver**: when poured out onto a flat tablet, though its drops are scattered here and there, it does not soak the surface with slippery moisture, nor does it stick to the boards. Instead, with incredible agility and unstable motion, it joins together again, and the small globules flow into one another and mass together. This occurs because their matter is dense, compressed, solid, and continuous—and of such density that it contains no air within itself. Because of this, it sinks to the very bottom, not only because of its weight but because it contains no airy substance. 

Likewise, **Agallochum** <note>Also known as Eaglewood or Aloeswood; a fragrant, resinous wood highly prized in the ancient world for incense and medicine</note>, or aloeswood, although it is light and of little weight, settles and sinks into the depths when immersed in water, because it is so compact that there is no empty space <note>original: "inane"; referring to a vacuum or void</note> within it.

### ¶ How meat and other foodstuffs may be preserved from rot in a shortage of salt. Incidentally, the wonderful power of Salt and vinegar. Chapter 36.

Everyone knows how useful and necessary the seasoning <note>original: "conditura"</note> of salt is to us. For besides the fact that Salt makes all food savory and most pleasing to the taste and palate, and stimulates an appetite for eating, it also rescues and protects all things from decay <note>original: "putrilagine"</note>. This is especially true of salt from which all muddy impurities have been boiled away and removed: for in that state it shines with a glittering color, and with it everything can be safely preserved and kept through much of the summer. It acts by absorbing and consuming all superfluous moisture <note>original: "excrementitium omnem humorem"; referring to excess fluids that lead to decomposition</note>, and it compresses and thickens meats and all salted provisions <note>original: "salsamenta"</note> so that no rot from the surrounding air can enter them. 

Furthermore, it may rightly seem a wonder to anyone that a certain power for fertility and for conquering sterility dwells within salt; indeed, even certain fields are made fertile by the sprinkling of it, which I have found by experience to be not far from the truth. Even obese women, who are for the most part barren <note>original: "effœtæ"</note>, may become fertile and fit for conception through the moderate use of salt in their seasonings. This is because salt wipes away all "swampy" dampness <note>original: "uliginem"</note> and dries out a womb that is more wet and soaked than is natural, ensuring that the genital seed may more easily cling to a uterus that has been rendered less slippery.

...sailors and fishermen are brought into port with the help [of salt], where they busily attend to their affairs. What power and capability vinegar possesses can be experienced from many things, but especially from this: an egg soaked in very sharp vinegar for three days, or a little more, becomes so soft in its shell <note>original: "teſta molleſcat"</note> that it can be passed through a narrow ring like a thin membrane. Even a small whetstone <note>original: "Coticula"</note> or a flint, mastered by vinegar over the space of seven days, is reduced to powder by the rub of a finger. Hence Hannibal, when he was making the Alps passable for himself and yearning for Italy, forced the rocks to dissolve and split apart with boiling vinegar <note>A reference to the famous legend from Livy's history, where the Carthaginian general Hannibal cleared a path through the Alps by heating the rocks and pouring vinegar over them to make them brittle.</note>.

### ON THE HIDDEN SECRETS OF NATURE
<meta>catchword: all-</meta>

The primary method for protecting and preserving health <term>valetudo</term> consists in temperance and moderation of food and drink. Since we have already treated the subject of dry nourishment and the eating of bread in abundance elsewhere, I thought it necessary to speak of drinking, and in what manner and measure each person should practice it. 

To begin with, nothing certain or definite can be prescribed to the healthy, since most people are accustomed to different drinking habits, which is easy for no one to change without loss or damage to their health. The best and safest way of drinking is determined for each according to their age, the nature of the seasons <note>original: "temporum ratione"</note>, their long-standing and ingrained habits, and the strength and potency of the wine. 

Thus, a drink of wine or another liquid should be prescribed to the thirsty to satisfy their desire, and so that the food is not left dry, nor floating in too much liquid, but is moderately moistened by the drink. Therefore, from time to time and at moderate intervals, the body should be refreshed by drinking, and the food should be repeatedly softened by the liquid poured over it, so that, once digestion <term>concoctio</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, digestion was viewed as a "cooking" process where the stomach's heat transformed food into a usable substance.</note> is completed, it may more conveniently enter the veins and be distributed throughout the body. 

All drunkenness <term>ebrietas</term>, especially if constant and continuous, is—according to the testimony of Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was a standard medical reference for centuries.</note>—destructive, because the nerves, besieged by copious wine every day, surrender <note>original: "dant manus"; a Latin idiom meaning to yield or give up</note>, and the entire structure of the body is loosened. Therefore, it is proper for drinking to be moderate

<margin>A comparison to butchers.</margin>

<margin>A comparison to the culinary arts.</margin>
For just as pots and cauldrons stop simmering and cease to boil when cold water is poured over them, so too the stomach, disturbed by an excessive drink, stops the digestion it has started, performs its duties later than it should, and digests the food less thoroughly. Thus, the food is propelled—undigested and before the proper time—either into the narrow passages of the veins or into the looseness of the intestines. From this, the use and benefit of the food is lost to the person, and through the obstruction of the internal organs—which leads to the rotting of the humors <term>humorum putredo</term> <note>The "humors" were the four primary bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health.</note>—it happens that the breeding grounds for diseases and fevers <term>febris</term> are summoned. This very thing also happens to those who, at the beginning and first reclining at the table, greedily gorge themselves with drink: for the food is immediately washed away...

## Chapter XLI.

The rays of the Sun and Moon exhibit certain and by no means ambiguous signs of clear weather, or rain, and of winds; these rays repeatedly take on various colors for themselves, either from the location and the circuit of the sky which they are accustomed to pass through, or from the nature of the object they strike, or from some matter poured over them. If those who thrust "Prognostics" <note>original: "Prognostica," refers to weather forecasts or astrological predictions often sold in cheap almanacs</note> upon the unskilled and unrefined common people and old women were to observe these signs accurately, it would not happen that they would wander so blindly or grope in the dark, nor would the credulous crowd be mocked with vain hope. For from these signs, imminent storms and whirlwinds can be predicted without doubt, as well as what the future state of the sky will be, from which we obtain either a rich abundance and crop of things, or a scarcity. Many other things are included in the elegant poem <margin>Virgil, *Georgics* Book 1</margin> of Virgil: who, since he was most skilled in the knowledge of things and followed all the works of nature exactly, also subjects the minds of men, in some part, to the forces and effects of those natural things. Indeed, according to the reckoning of time, the setting of the stars, the quality of the surrounding air, and the fourfold change of the year, men are affected differently and are constituted in different ways. ### ON MIRACLES. BOOK II.

...as much as the Sun irradiates with its own splendor; yet it fails and is rendered devoid of light whenever that light is blocked from it by the intervention of the Earth. It is at these times especially that the Moon unfolds its powers upon earthly things:

<margin>Opposition makes the **full moon**; conjunction makes the **new moon**.</margin>

either when it is filled and made into a perfect circle by being positioned directly opposite the Sun, or when it is first joined with it. During these periods of days, the crops grow, **shellfish** <note>original: "conchilia"; it was a common ancient belief that shellfish grew and shrank in size according to the lunar cycle</note> swell, and veins are filled with blood and bones with marrow. For this reason, it happens that **sexual intercourse** <note>original: "concubitus"</note> is less harmful at these times. And because the Moon saturates all things with moisture, it happens that meat exposed to its rays rots, and men who are overcome by sleep or wine contract a paleness and a heaviness of the head, and are afflicted by the **falling sickness** <term>falling sickness: an old name for epilepsy (Latin: "morbus comitialis"). It was called "comitial" because in ancient Rome, a seizure was seen as a divine omen that would immediately dissolve a public assembly, or "comitia."</term>. For it relaxes the nerves and moistens the brain more than is proper, and brings a stupor to the mind through its cold-inducing force.

<margin>The cause of the Ocean's **tides**.</margin>

Furthermore, there is no reason for anyone to doubt that the Moon stirs the tides of the Ocean and provides the cause for its ebbing and flowing. Indeed, we observe that when the Moon is silent and dark <note>the "silent" or "dark" moon refers to the New Moon phase when it is invisible</note>, or when it is divided into a half-circle, or curved into horns—whether it is waxing or waning—almost no surges of water occur, nor is the Ocean raised to any great height upon whatever shores it washes. On the other hand, when the Moon meets with the Sun and begins to be renewed, or is seen as a full circle, the greatest tides are stirred up and the waves are raised to an immense degree. Who could attribute this flux and reflux to anything other than the motion of the Moon?

...is driven now to this shore, now to that, and it inclines itself and settles upon that coast toward which the star [the Moon] is carried. I shall give some proof of this matter, and put forward examples of certain places, cities, and shores which the sea washes over.

First, so that everything may be understood exactly, I thought this **axiom** <term>axiom: a self-evident truth or a fundamental principle used as a starting point for reasoning.</term> or proposition should be set forth: the **Moon** always has its horns turned away from the **Sun**. If it is waxing, the horns face the East <note>original: "ortum"; the rising of the sun</note>; if it is waning, they face the West <note>original: "occasum"; the setting of the sun</note>. Having mostly dwelled in **conjunction** <term>conjunction: the moment when the Moon and Sun are in the same celestial longitude, making the Moon invisible from Earth (the "New Moon"). The author uses the term "coitu," literally a meeting or coming together.</term> for three days, it finally shines and flashes forth in a **crescent** <note>original: "falcata"; literally sickle-shaped</note> shape. 

Indeed, as it moves further from the Sun each day from its initial **increase** <note>original: "incremento"; referring to the waxing phase</note> until the seventh day, it is seen divided into a half-circle; that part is illuminated which is opposite the Sun as it moves toward the West, while that part remains dark which faces the East. For the waxing Moon always follows the setting Sun and is seen above our **horizon**. 

But when it wanes, it precedes the Sun and leads the way, and is seen above the horizon before dawn; that part is always illuminated which faces the Sun. Thus it happens that the curved part, shaped into horns, is always turned away from the Sun, while the rounded part, curved into a hump, faces and is exposed to the Sun. On the fourteenth day, when it is diametrically opposite the Sun, it becomes **full**, and it rises just as the Sun sinks into the West. In this way, it is illuminated from all sides and receives the Sun's brilliance from every direction.

On the seventeenth day, when the Sun rises, the Moon is seen low in the west. On the twenty-second day, after the Sun has emerged, the Moon travels through roughly the middle regions of the sky; that part which is turned toward the Sun is bright, while the rest remains dark. 

From then on, as it follows its course day by day, it finally completes the entire circle of the **zodiac** <term>zodiac: literally the "sign-bearing circle" (*signifer circulus*); the belt of the heavens through which the sun and moon appear to move.</term> on the twenty-eighth day and a third part of a day—that is, eight hours. And just as the Sun completes a year, so the Moon completes a month, with the changes occurring in seven-day intervals <note>original: "per septimanas"; referring to the four weekly phases of the lunar cycle</note>. 

For both periods are completed in seven days: the time after its first appearance when it waxes into a half-circle, and the time from there until it becomes full and is rounded into a perfect circle <note>original: "rotundū circinatur"; literally "rounded as if by a compass"</note>. These periods, when doubled, constitute fourteen days. In a similar way, if you calculate the time from when the Moon is divided into equal portions [the half-moon] to the second such division [the waning half-moon], and then the remaining days until the Moon has completely vanished from our sight, you will find segments of seven days. 

Therefore, it is clear that the month is governed by the changes of the Moon. The Moon gains this power from its relationship to the Sun <note>original: "à Solis aspectu"; literally "from the sight/aspect of the Sun"</note>, for it is endowed with no such powers or forces of its own. But when it enters into **conjunction** <term>conjunction: here "congressum," the meeting of the Sun and Moon in the sky (New Moon).</term> with the Sun, or is fully illuminated from the opposite side [Full Moon], violent changes are brought upon the land and sea; the proof of this is that it stirs up impetuous winds and beats against the shores with frequent waves. On the day the new Moon is sighted (which always hangs in the West, because the Sun—by whose brilliance the moon begins to shine—is setting there) and on the day it becomes full, we observe that the tides <note>original: "æstus," the rhythmic swelling and surging of the sea</note> are stirred up and spread abroad. ### ¶ *On the herb Great Water-Dock, commonly called Patience. Chapter 43.*

<margin>Sorrel</margin> <note>original: "Zurckel," a Dutch/Low German term for sorrel or dock.</note>
Since there are many kinds of <term>Rumex</term> <note>The genus containing docks and sorrels</note> or Dock, two are especially sought after for eating. First is *Oxalis*, commonly called *Acedula* or *Acetosa* <note>Common Sorrel</note>, which sharpens the appetite in salads and dispels nausea. The second is *Hippolapathon* <note>Great Water-Dock, literally "Horse-dock"</note>, so named for its great size. It is a stalky vegetable with large, very long leaves; the stalk is reddish when it has matured, and the root is yellowish. I have found by experience that this herb has the following power: meats and any other foods, no matter how aged or very old they may be, become tender when boiled with it and are rendered fit for eating. For since it is of a slippery and moist nature, it softens and tenderizes even the toughest beef or poultry. Because of this, its use was frequent among the ancients, as it makes foods easy to digest and softens the bowels. Of the same power as this is *Atriplex* <note>Orach or Saltbush</note>, and that which is called *Spinacia* <note>Spinach</note> from its prickly seed; I believe *Martial* <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams</note> was referring to this when he said:
> *Use lettuce, and use the soft mallows.*
<note>original: "Vtere lactucis, & mollibus vtere maluis." Martial, Epigrams 3.89</note>

And finally *Horace* <note>A leading Roman lyric poet</note> mentions it:
> *Olives gathered from the richest*
> *branches of the trees,*
> *or the herb of the dock that loves the meadows, and*
> *mallows healthy for the body.*
<note>original: "Lecta de pinguissimis / Oliua ramis arborum, / Aut herba lapathi prata amantis, & graui / Malua salubres corpori." Horace, Epodes 2.55-58</note>

<header>### ON WONDERS. BOOK II.</header>

The use of milk is not equally healthy for everyone; indeed, for those who have a **colder stomach**, it turns sour and distends the <term>internal organs</term> <note>original: "præcordia," the area around the heart and diaphragm</note> with gas. But for those who possess a **warmer temperament** of the body, the milk is scorched, evaporates into smoky fumes, and brings a heaviness to the head. 

And since milk is of such a nature that it thickens and solidifies with heat, but liquefies with cold, it happens that it curdles more readily in a burning stomach. This curdling is prevented by nothing more effectively than by **honey**, or **sugar**, and a tiny bit of salt. 

Furthermore, since I have known many people to be strangled by curdled milk—solidified into lumps—because the breathing passage was blocked by the onset of vomiting, it seems to me that some playful young girls and bold suitors act unwisely; in afternoon banquets, they stuff themselves with <term>beastings</term> <note>original: "colostris," the first milk of a mammal after giving birth, which is especially thick</note>, cream, and other dairy products, and do not fear to douse them abundantly with **wine**, to the greatest detriment of their health. 

For wine causes milk to clump and glob together into the consistency of cheese. When the stomach is burdened by this and is unable to process or digest the resistant mass, everything tends toward rot, providing a breeding ground for great illnesses. Thus, fish and milk, and all acidic things mixed with milk and drenched with wine, produce <term>scabies</term> and <term>leprosy</term> <note>In the 16th century, "leprosy" and "scabies" often served as general terms for various severe or contagious skin diseases and imbalances of the humors</note>. ### *¶ That wine is spoiled by thunder and lightning, as well as that liquid which is called Beer by the Belgians; and by what means this may be prevented, and how their strengths may be restored. Chapter 49.*

That thunder and lightning bring harm to the pantry <note>original: "rei penuariæ"</note> and the wine cellars is something every head of a household has experienced to his own clear loss. Indeed, wine grows flat <note>original: "vapescit," suggesting it loses its "spirit" or life and becomes like vapor</note> due to lightning, takes on a reddish-brown color, and its genuine flavor is destroyed by the fiery heat and its penetrating, burning power. **Beer** <note>original: "Ceruisia"</note> is spoiled by sourness due to that horrific sound, violent movement, and shaking, and is rendered unfit for drinking. And although summer heat is the primary cause for liquids turning sour, lightning and thunder nevertheless bring a sudden change to such things even in the winter months, whereas heat does so gradually. ...the harshness of the air and the breeze falls more violently upon the wine jars and casks. For it leaves thin and soft things untouched, because a passage lies open through them and the lightning does not cling to them. Thus we see that the oak and the holm-oak—being the hardest and tallest trees—are most exposed to the injury of lightning, while the **Laurel** tree, which yields to it and does not resist, is seen to remain untouched. So it has been proven by experience rather than by theory that the skin of a **Seal** <margin>seal</margin> <note>original: "Phocæ"; the Dutch margin note "zeehonde" confirms this refers to a seal</note> or "sea-calf" is unconquered by lightning—I suppose because its texture is thin and less solid—and the same is true for the **Eagle** and its remains <note>original: "exuvias"; refers to the feathers or skin of the bird</note>.

Furthermore, it is in everyone's interest to know, and useful to remember for the sake of their health, that foods spoiled by lightning are harmful and destructive. For there is a pestilential power within lightning, from which a poisonous spirit is spread into everything it touches. This is why a most foul odor emanates from things scorched by lightning; we perceive this in rubbed ears of grain, <margin>commonly called blight</margin> <note>original: "Brandt"; a term for fungal smut or blight in crops, here attributed to lightning</note> which, having been spoiled by the touch of lightning's rot, pour a sulfurous smell into the nostrils. ### ¶ Omens of storms from contact with seawater, and what winter thunder portends. Chapter 49.

I have often observed, while being carried in a skiff to more distant shores, that if I immerse my hand in the brine, the seawater feels entirely lukewarm and imbued with heat. This itself portends that a storm is imminent within three days, bringing violent winds and powerful waves. For when a storm settles upon the deep and remote sea from which the tide is carried to us, the seawater becomes struck and agitated, growing warm—just as hands grow hot when clapped together <note>The author uses a common early modern analogy: just as friction creates heat between hands, the "friction" of a distant storm heats the ocean water before the wind arrives</note>. Soon, whirlwinds and tempests are rolled down toward us, and the waves swell to their greatest height. Similarly, if ever thunder breaks out during the winter months, and the sky flashes with lightning, or the heavens shimmer with frequent fires, it is a sign that a coming storm and "Typhonic" winds <note>original: "Typhonicos"; referring to hurricane-force winds or severe circular storms associated with the mythological monster Typhon</note> will follow...

# ON THE SECRETS OF NATURE

If a grapevine becomes sterile and produces nothing but leaves, runners, and shoots, it can be made fertile again if it is drenched with <term>sharp and aged urine</term> <note>original: "lotio acri ac vetusto." In early modern agriculture, aged urine was used as a nitrogen-rich fertilizer to stimulate growth.</note>. Since the vine is often "choked" by an overabundance of moisture, the application of urine excites its internal heat and draws out the excess, waste-like humidity, causing the vine to swell with beautiful and abundant fruit. This same effect can also be achieved by pouring wine dregs <note>original: "fece vini"</note> onto the roots. However, our local people provide for the fertility of the vine poorly: they dig a trench and bury <term>soot</term> <note>original: "fuliginem"</note> scraped from the chimney around the roots. Even though there seems to be some richness or "fatness" in that soot, its burning and scorching quality actually brings ruin to the vineyard and causes it to wither.

<term>Clary Sage</term> <note>original: "Orminum." Specifically *Salvia sclarea*, traditionally known as "Clear-eye."</note> is called "Cock’s Spur" in the apothecary shops. Its seed has an attractive power that removes bits of straw, dust, and other irritants that fall into the eyes. Indeed, when the seed is placed in the eye, it rolls all around the surface; once it has absorbed the moisture and cleared away any "fog" or dimness, it comes out swollen and covered as if by a thin membrane. The herb itself, when crushed, extracts stingers and thorns, and it accelerates lingering or difficult labors in childbirth. When cast into wine, it cheers the mind, scatters the "clouds" of the soul, and stimulates desire; however, if taken too liberally, its heavy scent attacks the head <note>meaning it causes headaches or a sense of intoxication.</note>. A decoction of <term>Marshmallow</term> <note>original: "Altheæ"</note> and <term>Mallow</term> <note>original: "Maluæ"</note> softens and soothes rough, wrinkled hands; even more effective for this purpose is <term>Fenugreek</term> <note>original: "Fœni græci"</note>,

It has seemed to some like a kind of miracle that certain sick people have very hot limbs and a body burning all over, and yet are not oppressed by any thirst. This occurs because the heat diffuses itself throughout the body and does not fix itself upon the heart or any other governing organ. Thus it happens that when sweat breaks out and the heart is able to "breathe," and the smoky heat that occupied the internal organs is scattered, the patients cease to be thirsty. On the other hand, those in whom the heat does not break out to the outer skin but remains hidden within are tortured by an intolerable thirst, even if no outward signs of heat display themselves.

It will happen that the wine is imbued with such coldness that the teeth can hardly bear it. Furthermore, it is the quality of this substance that creates that great report in **cannons** <term>bombardis</term>; however, if it were removed, there would be no sound, nor would the shot be fired with such force.

# ON THE SECRET THINGS OF NATURE
<meta>catchword: -nidas (completing the word "euanidas" from the end of the page)</meta>

<margin>
How wine is to be diluted.
</margin>

If anyone decides to drink more dilutedly, and considers it prudent that wine which is overly pure <note>original: "meracũ"; referring to wine that is undiluted or "neat."</note> should be softened by pouring in water, they ought not to attempt this while eating, but rather an hour and a half before they are to sit down for a meal. In this way, the liquids blend together, and they do not resist digestion through conflicting qualities. Indeed, when diluted in the common fashion <note>i.e., mixing water and wine at the table right before drinking.</note>, they affect the head and stir up rumbling and gas. Sour wines and those that are slightly harsh should not be mixed with sweet ones, nor should red wine be mixed with white. For foods of differing qualities create trouble for the stomach: since one may be hurried into the body's system more quickly, while another is absorbed more slowly. For this reason, I advise that this choice be made: that white wine be taken at lunch <note>original: "prandio"</note>, but red at dinner. For white wine flows down easily and makes the veins and urinary passages open and dilated; red wine, however—provided it is of a noble sort—is more nourishing, but it possesses an astringent <note>original: "astrictionis"; a drying or puckering quality.</note> quality. But if both are drunk at the same table, the white should always be served before the red. Furthermore, while I believe the method of diluting wine should not be entirely neglected, that saying of Plutarch has always pleased me:

> It is better to drink wine moderately at the proper time, than to dilute it with water; for the wine is spoiled by the water poured into it.

<margin>
How chestnuts may be preserved.
</margin>

If anyone wishes to keep chestnuts <note>original: "Castaneas"</note> unspoiled, let him sprinkle in "royal nuts" <term>nuces basilicas</term> gathered from the walnut tree <note>original: "iuglande"; the writer suggests storing chestnuts among walnuts to maintain their freshness.</note>. For these [the walnuts] draw out all the dampness and superfluous moisture which makes the chestnuts rot and decay...

### ON MIRACLES. BOOK II.

<margin>
Walnut medicine.
</margin>
...absorbs the fading [moistures] and prevents them from being covered by decay. For it is the nature of the walnut <note>original: "nux regia," literally "the royal nut"</note> to dry out and consume moisture; for this reason, it is used healthfully for the tonsils, the uvula, and all ailments of the throat. For this purpose, the *Diacaryon* <note>original: "Diacaryon"; a Greek-derived term meaning "made of nuts."</note>—that is, an antidote made from nuts—is prepared, which stops and represses all discharges <note>original: "fluxiones"; referring to excess mucus or catarrh</note> from the head. 

<margin>
Antidote.
</margin>
And since walnuts resist poisons and disperse the contagions of tainted air, the "four-fold" <note>original: "diatessaron"; a remedy named for its four primary ingredients.</note> composition was devised by the ancients. It calls for two walnuts and the same number of figs, twenty leaves of rue, and a few grains of salt; if anyone takes these crushed together while fasting, they shall be immune to poisons and contagious diseases on that day.

<margin>
The Onion.
</margin>
The onion, contrary to the nature of all other plants, increases and takes on growth when the Moon is waning, but decreases when the Moon is waxing. This happens because the Moon chokes it with excessive moisture. For since the onion is juicy by nature, as are all bulbous plants, and is abundantly filled with its own native sap, the waxing Moon increases its moisture but diminishes its heat—and heat is the primary reason that plants achieve growth. 

By the same reasoning, those who are enormously fat and obese are sterile and do not reproduce, because they lack the heat which makes the female reproductive matter <note>original: "excrementum feminale"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the female contribution to conception.</note> fertile and prolific. And this is why onions, aloe, navelwort <note>original: "acetabulum"</note>, saffron root, squill <note>a type of sea onion</note>, leeks, and many other things swollen with their native juice, when fixed to the rafters of a larder <note>original: "carnario"; a place for hanging meat</note>...

<margin>
The hungry at the onset of fever.
</margin>
Fevers that make men gluttonous <note>original: "edaces," meaning those with a voracious appetite.</note> tend to be long-lasting; therefore, it has always seemed better to me for those with fevers to be thirsty rather than hungry. For the former, since their fever is ignited from yellow bile <note>original: "flaua bili"; in humorism, yellow bile was associated with heat, dryness, and choleric temperaments.</note>, they easily soften when a large amount of liquid is poured in and sweat is aroused. But for the latter, who are greedy for food, the fever is aroused from the melancholic humor <note>The "black bile," associated with cold and dry properties.</note> and from acid and salty phlegm <note>original: "pituita."</note>. When the stomach is drenched in these humors, they are led by an irrational desire for eating; thus it happens that those so affected nourish the disease, provide fuel <note>original: "fomitem," literally "tinder."</note> for it, and struggle longer with the fever. Since there are three types of phlegm, as Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories of humors dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> witnesses: sweet, acid, and 
<margin>
On fullness.
</margin>
salty. The first makes one sleepy, the second hungry, and the third thirsty. Of all these, the type that makes men gluttonous produces the longest-lasting diseases. Therefore, if you wish to terminate these illnesses more quickly, withdraw food at the onset <note>original: "inſultu," referring to the attack or paroxysm of the disease.</note> of the sickness.

### ON MIRACLES. BOOK II.

...you draw it out, always allow it to sink right down to the bottom until the vessel is empty; the wine will neither degenerate nor go flat. For all those things which might bring some defect to it settle upon the dregs <note>original: "suillam," referring to the heavy sediment or lees at the bottom of the wine jar.</note>. Meanwhile, the opening of the jar ought to be closed very tightly, so that no air may enter, and it should be secured with a small bag filled either with salt or with damp sand. For in this way, the wine will neither go flat nor contract any sourness.

Moreover, so that slightly sour wine or vinegar might take on the nature of wine again, you may achieve this with leek seeds, or by throwing in vine shoots and tendrils <note>original: "pampinis ac capreolis."</note>.

Corrupted and viscous <note>original: "glutinosum," referring to a ropey or thick texture in spoiled wine caused by bacterial growth.</note> wine is restored with slightly salted cow’s milk. There are some who attempt this with lime, sulfur, and alum; however, so that these are not harmful to humans or cause injury, I recommend that the root of an Iris <note>original: "Iridis radicem"; Orris root was often used as a stabilizer and flavoring.</note> and juniper berries should be mixed in.

To make the wine pleasing to the palate, acceptable, and agreeable in scent and color: you should place a Median apple <note>original: "malum Medicum," usually referring to a citron (*Citrus medica*).</note>—that is, a citron fruit—studded all over with cloves <note>original: "gariophyllis"</note> into the jar in such a way that it does not touch the wine; for it would rot from the moisture, and the wine will contract no vapid or moldy flavor.

### ON THE HIDDEN SECRETS OF NATURE

...we perceive to germinate; for when they are sufficiently saturated with juice, they only need heat to leap forth and bring themselves out.

<margin>Hunger during an attacking fever.</margin>
Fevers that make men gluttonous <note>original: "edaces"; the author refers to a condition called "bulimia" or "canine appetite" often described in early modern medicine as a symptom of specific fevers.</note> tend to be long-lasting; therefore, it has always seemed better to me for feverish patients to be thirsty rather than hungry. For in those [the thirsty], since the fever is kindled by yellow bile, they easily recover through an abundance of fluids and the stirring of sweat; but in those who are greedy for food, the fever is stirred up from a melancholic humor and from acid and salty phlegm <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four vital bodily humors, which was thought to cause disease if it became "corrupt" or changed in flavor.</note>. When the stomach is flooded with these humors, they are led by an unreasonable desire to eat; thus it happens that those so affected nourish the disease, provide it with fuel <note>original: "fomitem," literally "tinder."</note>, and struggle with the fever for a longer time.
