# ON THE SECRETS OF NATURE

->...poisons, and the contagions of diseases.<-

In Italy, physicians obtain criminals who have been condemned to death from the governors at certain times of the year for the purpose of dissection, so that students of medicine may be trained in the study of <term>Anatomy</term> <note>original: "Anatomica"; the practice of dissecting bodies to understand the human structure, which was becoming more regulated in the Renaissance.</note>. Therefore, so that no <term>humors</term> <note>According to the medical theory of the time, "humors" were the vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that governed health.</note> are scattered or the thicker spirits allowed to vanish, and so that all parts may reveal themselves clearly, they give the condemned two or three drachms of <margin>The power of Opium.</margin> **Opium**—that is, the black juice of the poppy—mixed with very pure wine. Once this potion has been drunk, they first begin to grow cheerful, as if bathed in a <term>sardonic laugh</term> <note>original: "risu Sardonio"; a convulsive, grimace-like grin often associated with poisoning or impending death.</note>; soon, they are released into a heavy, deep sleep and are lulled into death. Indeed, the drug seizes the veins and vital organs with such speed that, when the bodies of those drugged with Opium are dissected, it has been found that the substance has clung to the heart.

<margin>The method of making vinegar</margin> If wine or beer exposed to the sun and wind are slow to turn sour, crushed salt mixed with pepper and a slightly sour leaven will achieve this very quickly. But if you wish to accomplish this even more hastily, throw a piece of steel or a brick that has been heated in the fire once or twice into the vessel, or submerge radish roots; they will immediately contract an acidic sharpness. Also medlars, unripe cornelian cherries, blackberries—whether gathered from the bramble or the tree—and wild sloes cut here and there, and <margin>Morello cherries <note>original: "Merellen"; a common name for dark, sour cherries.</note></margin> **Actian cherries** <note>A variety of cherry mentioned by ancient naturalists, likely originating from the region of Actium.</note> which are covered in a black color on the outside but are blood-red within, will imbue liquids with an acidic flavor and a most exuberant red color...

For that wild poppy, familiar in grain fields, stains liquids with a worm-red and scarlet hue; but its use is harmful and dangerous, so that the error of those who offer either a decoction, a dilution, or finally a distilled liquid of this for <term>angina</term> <note>original: "angina"; in this period, it referred broadly to inflammations of the throat or neck that caused choking, rather than specifically heart-related pain.</note> and side pain <note>original: "dolore laterali"; likely referring to pleurisy.</note> must be rejected, since it is astringent in nature and narcotic—that is, inducing stupor—and does not encourage the coughing up of phlegm.

<margin>A method for examining Leprosy.</margin>
**Elephantiasis**, which is commonly designated by the name of **leprosy**, is an abominable and foul disease, and for that reason, those contaminated by it are banished outside the city boundaries. And since it is sometimes difficult to recognize, certain Judges and Examiners have been appointed among the Belgians <note>The author, Lemnius, was a Dutch physician; "Belgians" here refers to the inhabitants of the Low Countries.</note> to examine these people. I perform a test using urine, into which I sprinkle the ashes of burnt lead: if they sink and fall to the bottom of the vessel, there is no contagion of this disease in the body; but if they float and stick to the surface of the urine, I determine the person is infected. For this indicates a thickness of the humors and a <term>burnt</term> and corrupted melancholy <note>original: "melancholiam"; according to the theory of the four humors, "black bile" (melancholy) could become "burnt" (adust) through excess heat, leading to severe physical and mental diseases.</note> diffused throughout the entire body.
